Antagonistic pairs are pairs of muscles that perform the opposite movements, and are the agonist/antagonist pairs for each different movement. Generally you’ll find antagonistic pairs on opposite sides of the body.
For example, biceps and triceps are an antagonistic pair.

During forearm flexion (bending your arm at the elbow), biceps in shortening, and triceps is relaxing/lengthening to allow this movement. In this case, biceps is the agonist (prime moving, causing the movement) and triceps is the antagonist (opposes/does the opposite movement).

During forearm extension (straightening your arm at the elbow), biceps is relaxing/lengthening and triceps is shortening. In this case, biceps is the antagonist (opposes/does the opposite movement) and triceps is the agonist (prime mover, causing the movement).

Every muscle cells has its own neuromuscular junction – this is where the nerve can stimulate the muscle to contract. So you can choose how many muscle fibers in a muscle to contract, to make variable amounts of force.
In order for muscle contraction to occur, you must have the following:
Acetyl Choline – main neurotransmitter for muscle contraction – needed for contraction.
ATP – energy used by the muscle for contraction
Calcium and Magnesium – co factors for contraction – without these, the muscles can’t use ATP
Organisation of muscle fibres and muscle coverings in skeletal muscle

Myofibrils are made up of myofilaments – strands of actin and myosin, the proteins that allow the muscle to contract by interacting. Together the myofibrils create the muscle fibre (or muscle cell, these terms are interchangeable.).
The muscle as a whole has a similar bundle type arrangement, with connective tissue coverings (instead of sarcolemma and mitochondria!).

Spinal Nerves and the Spinal Cord

The spinal cord and spinal nerves represent one of the transition points from CNS to PNS. The spinal cord is comprised for grey and white matter, and I like to imagine it as looking like a butterfly within an overdrawn set of lips! It's certainly a stretch but can you see it?

The butterfly is the grey matter - this is where the cell bodies of neurons are, and you can see the grey matter is found in the middle, the opposite to the brain! The lips are the white matter tracts, the axons of those neurons connecting the brain to the body! On the image below it shows the different parts of the white matter, the nerve tracts, with the blue part carrying information TO the brain, and the red parts carrying information FROM the brain. You can see it's very distinctly organised! It is not important to remember these tracts, I just wanted you to see how specific each part of the nervous system is!
The spinal nerves are associated with the vertebrae of the spinal column, with the spinal nerves exiting the spinal cord and moving into the body/nerve plexuses through the spaces between vertebrae.
At this junction you have nerves exiting the vertebral column along with blood vessels. This area is an important structure for understanding about reflexes and the reflex arc!

Below you can see how the spinal nerves is arranged, carrying both somatic (voluntary) and visceral (involuntary) motor nerves to control the body. There are two images, showing slightly different views of what the nerve looks like! Both of these examples would be for a nerve of the sympathetic nervous system, and preganglionic fibres as part of the autonomic nervous systems!
The Autonomic nervous system; which covers the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system includes SOME but not ALL of the peripheral nerves. The image below shows the origins of the SNS and PSNS

The PSNS has a craniosacral origin - from 4 cranial nerves (3, 7, 9 and 10) and 3 sacral spinal nerves (S2-S4). The SNS has what we call a thoracolumbar origin - from T1-L2, the thoracic and lumbar nerves, and forms a chain of sympathetic ganglia (a ganglion/ganglia is just a group of neurons!)

While there are 31 spinal nerves, there is not an exact one to one relationship with the vertebrae, partly due to the fusion of vertebrae to form the tailbone. The spinal cord has some changes in structure too, forming the cauda equina, named because it looks a bit like a horses tail.

The reflex arc allows the peripheral nervous system to stimulate predictable action in the body. What I mean by this that a reflex is a consistent response to a particular stimulus. Since the response is consistent, the same every time, you can hardwire it into the spinal cord, so you don't need the brain involved in that decision. We do this using interneurons. Gustation (our sense of taste) and Olfaction (our sense of smell) are caleld chemical senses, as they involve receptors on sensory neurons binding to chemical compounds and sending signals to our brains for processing. These are one of the ways that we get information about our world, and chemical senses are thought to be the oldest kind of sense in the world. Even bacteria have the ability to sense the chemicals in the environment around them. For humans, we tend to think of these are less important senses, as we rely heavily on vision and hearing, but, these senses are still important and amazing processes!

The Olfactory Bulb are two structures of the brain that lay on the underside of the brain, and neurons from the olfactory bulbs poke down, through the skull into the roof of the nasal cavity, where volatile compounds (those things that we smell) come into contact with the receptors on the neurons!

An interesting thing about the olfactory bulb is that the neurons are able to be replaced, and are part of something called the rostral migratory stream, where stem cells from the subventricular zone (near the ventricles of the brain) grow and divide to create cells that will travel to the olfactory bulb to replace old cells. 22. Complete the genetics glossary below. They are in no particular order, and some related words are close together in the list, or further apart!

The process of cell division that results in _____________ identical (but not necessarily functionally identical) daughter cells. These daughter cells will have _______________chromosomes (______________pairs), and they will be diploid (having ___________ set of chromosomes, 1 maternal and 1 paternal).

The process of cell division that results in ______________ genetically varied daughter cells that function as gametes (egg cells and sperm cells). Only occurs in your _________________, and each daughter cell will have 23 chromosomes (1 set) and haploid (1 set chromosomes).

The fact that humans have ____________________, and their complement of genes (that make up their genome) can be very different to others. This variation is important for health and wellbeing. When populations have low genetic variation, they can be more susceptible to disease and genetic issues.
A sequence of ___________ that codes for a protein. That protein will carry out a function in the body!
The genetic material that contains all the instructions for the body's function.
DNA isn't found by itself, in the nucleus, it is package up and wound around special proteins. These proteins and DNA together are called chromatin.
A chromosome is a ______________that is inherited together - certain genes are found on certain chromosomes! Humans have 46 chromosomes, 23 from mum and 23 from dad.
A chromosome that is not a _______chromosome and so does not contribute to genetic sex. Autosomes in humans are numbered 1-22

A chromosome that contributes to genetic sex. In humans these are the ___________ chromosomes, and most people have 2, a pair of sex chromosomes, with an X from mum, and either an X or Y from dad (but there are other genetic sex combos as well!).
A cell with only ________ of each chromosome. Our gametes (eggs and sperm) are haploid and have 23 chromosomes
A cell with __________ of each chromosome. Our body cells are diploid and have 23 pairs of chromosomes, for a total of 46 chromosomes.

When a person has an abnormal ________of chromsomes - usually an extra, or missing 1. There are a few different aneuploidies, but common ones are Down Syndrome (or Trisomy 21 when a person inherits an extra chromosome 21), Turners syndrome (when a person have only 1 sex chromosome and so their genetic sex is XO), or Klinefelters syndrome (when a person has 2 X chromosomes and 1 Y chromsome).

Polyploid is when something has ______________ SETS of chromosomes, and can be triploid (3 copies of each chromosome), tetraploid (4) and so on. This is very rare in human reproduction, but can occur in liver and placenta cells!

Disjunction is when chromosomes divide during meiosis. In meiosis 2, sister chromatids that make up a chromosome are split into 2 new chromosomes, and end up in different gametes. When this doesn't happen properly, it is called non-disjunction, and gametes end up with extra chromosomes or missing chromosomes (ie 1 gametes gets 2 chromosomes, and the other gamete made in the same division gets none!)
The process by which a cell splits into two new cells. The parent cells must be large enough and have duplicates of their DNA and organelles so the two new cells have their own machinery.
The different stages of mitosis (and meiosis)
In humans, this is a haploid _____________ cell that will be used for sexual reproduction - a male and female gamete join to create a zygote!

A version of a gene that is always expressed in a _____________________ (the traits/things that we see in our body). The dominant allele is like your loud friend, if they are there, you're always going to hear them!

A version of a gene that you only see in the phenotype or trait of a person if there is none of the dominant version in other words when there are ___________ recessive ones. The reccessive allele is like that friend you have that everyone think is shy and quiet, but as soon as everyone leaves, they turn into the nutjob you know and love :)

When you have codominance, you have 2 dominant alleles. So that is like having two loud friends, and they just talk over each other all the time! There are traits we have where 2 version can be expressed at the same time. The best example is human blood groups. A and B alleles are both _______________, which is why you have A blood, B blood AND AB blood which has both. O blood group is the __________________!

Incomplete dominance is when you have two alleles, and neither one is really properly dominant. A good example is flowers, where you have a red version, and a white version of the gene for colour, but when you have BOTH versions you end up with ____________! SO not quite red, not quite white. You dont see this much in humans, Sickle Cell disease is really the only example. In Sickle cell disease, if you have both a normal gene and a disease gene, half your RBCS are sickle shaped and half are normal. This mix means a person won't have the symptoms of sickle cell disease (which is bad), but! they are resistant to malaria!
When ___________gene creates a trait. Some examples of monogenic traits are: Attached or unattached ear lobes, middle digit hair, where there distinct options, or groups of traits.

When _______________ genes create a trait. Some examples of polygenetic traits are things that have a spectrum, like height, body size, hair colour, body shape, eye colour, voice, skin colour - there isn't necessarily specific groups, e.g. blonde vs brown is subjective.

Are what we call the different versions of genes, and they can be recessive or dominant! For example, a gene could have a normal and diseased version - they would each be alleles. We commonly use eye colour alleles to think about this too.
These are the genes you got. Your genetic makeup. For example, a person might have an A allele and an O allele for their blood type.
This is the trait you have - what is expressed. The person above, with AO alleles for blood type would have Type A Blood.
The trait is something that you are inheriting from your parents, and it based on your genes
Mutation is caused when something causes your DNA to __________. Things like UV rays can cause mutations in your DNA sequence.
When an ________ and ___________join together, they form a zygote, the beginning of a new organism.
When you have two alleles that are the _________
When you have two alleles that are ______________
A methods to figure out what genotypes are possible in children of two parents
A family tree of the genes of different people. We can use these to figure out the genotypes of different people in a family based on the phenotypes of different people.
A diploid complement of homologous chromosomes - all the chromosomes you have in each cell!
Your mitochondria have their own DNA! People only inherit their mitochondrial DNA from their mum, so mitochondrial DNA diseases only pass from mother to child. There is an article here
Article: Sperm Mitophagy and Mitochondrial DNA
about how any sperm mitochondria is destroyed so only egg mitochondria are found in the new zygote!
When you have 3 copies of a chromosome when you should only have two. The most common trisomy is Trisomy 21, or Down's Syndrome

A genetic testing protocol, where a part of the placenta (called the chorionic villus) is extracted from the uterus for genetic testing. The chorionic villus has the same DNA as the fetus (as it is made from cells that come from the zygote).
A genetic testing protocol where some of the amniotic fluid is removed from the uterus for genetic testing.
The idea that we can replace mutated or diseases genes in a person with the normal, non diseased gene, or in some way correct genetic abnormalities.

which means to secrete. 8. How is glucose stored in the body, and where?

Just like your kitchen, you have 3 places to put glucose. The pantry is for short term storage (for ready to eats, or snacks!) where the glucose is easily available, the fridge for longer term storage (where you put ingredients, things you gotta do stuff to to make a meal), for use over the day inbetween meals, and the deep freezer, where you store things for a LONG time, and only utilse once you've run out of the easy stuff (like when you freexe leftovers for when you can't be bothered cooking, or you store a ham cos you got in cheap and are saving it for Christmas).

The pantry of your body is your muscle, which stores glucose as glycogen (the storage form of glucose, which creates long branching chains, kind of like starch!). The glycogen in your muscles can be used BY your muscles, and is immediately available once it is broken down. Kind of like having snacks in your pocket!

The fridge of your body is the liver - the liver stores glucose as glycogen as well but does so for the rest of the body, so inbetween meals, your liver can release glucose into your blood for the other parts of your body to use. That nagging hungry feeling you get after a few hours is normally your liver singalling that it's running out of stored glucose!

The deep freeze of your body is your fat. Glucose is converted into fatty acids for long term storage, as your can store more calories as fat than as glycogen in the same amount of space. They can be made from amino acids, polypeptides or proteins and cannot cross the cell membrane, so need a cell surface receptor, and create a intracellular cascade (it is kind of the equivalent of someone coming to your door and shouting instructions!). Steroid hormones are lipid soluble, so are able to diffuse through the cell membrane and enter cells. This means that they don't need a cell surface receptor and instead can travel to the nucleus where they change gene activation. The process of cell division that results in 2 genetically identical (but not necessarily functionally identical) daughter cells. These daughter cells will have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs), and they will be diploid (having 2 set of chromosomes, 1 maternal and 1 paternal).

The process of cell division that results in 4 genetically varied daughter cells that function as gametes (egg cells and sperm cells). Only occurs in your gonads, and each daughter cell will have 23 chromosomes (1 set) and haploid (1 set chromosomes).

The fact that humans have different versions of genes, and their complement of genes (that make up their genome) can be very different to others. This variation is important for health and wellbeing. When populations have low genetic variation, they can be more susceptible to disease and genetic issues.
A sequence of DNA that codes for a protein. That protein will carry out a function in the body!
The genetic material that contains all the instructions for the body's function.
DNA isn't found by itself, in the nucleus, it is package up and wound around special proteins. These proteins and DNA together are called chromatin.
A chromosome is a length of DNA that is inherited together - certain genes are found on certain chromosomes! Humans have 46 chromosomes, 23 from mum and 23 from dad.
A chromosome that is not a sex chromosome and so does not contribute to genetic sex. Autosomes in humans are numbered 1-22

A chromosome that contributes to genetic sex. In humans these are the X and Y chromosome, and most people have 2, a pair of sex chromosomes, with an X from mum, and either an X or Y from dad (but there are other genetic sex combos as well!).
A cell with only one of each chromosome. Our gametes (eggs and sperm) are haploid and have 23 chromosomes
A cell with 2 of each chromosome. Our body cells are diploid and have 23 pairs of chromosomes, for a total of 46 chromosomes.

When a person has an abnormal number of chromsomes - usually an extra, or missing 1. There are a few different aneuploidies, but common ones are Down Syndrome (or Trisomy 21 when a person inherits an extra chromosome 21), Turners syndrome (when a person have only 1 sex chromosome and so their genetic sex is XO), or Klinefelters syndrome (when a person has 2 X chromosomes and 1 Y chromsome).

Polyploid is when something has multiple SETS of chromosomes, and can be triploid (3 copies of each chromosome), tetraploid (4) and so on. This is very rare in human reproduction, but can occur in liver and placenta cells!

Disjunction is when chromosomes divide during meiosis. In meiosis 2, sister chromatids that make up a chromosome are split into 2 new chromosomes, and end up in different gametes. When this doesn't happen properly, it is called non-disjunction, and gametes end up with extra chromosomes or missing chromosomes (ie 1 gametes gets 2 chromosomes, and the other gamete made in the same division gets none!)

left381000Blast: to build (builder cells, make things).
Clast: to destroy (reabsorb tissue, breaks things)

Blasts and clasts are constantly working together to change the bone tissue. They respond to changes in the amount of calcium in the body (because bones store calcium) and they also respond to changes in the amount of force on the body.
So if your body has to hold up MORE force, the bones must get stronger/denser, and if your body needs to hold up LESS force, the bones CAN get less dense
Cyte: a generic cell, helps to maintain and keep bone alive, but does not create or destroy bone.
Compact bone has circular osteon arranged together, kind of like spaghetti that is stacked together in a bundle. The blood supply is in the centre of the osteon.

left10901800Spongy or trabecular (branching) bone provides support inside the bone, but is porous and light, to allow the bones to be a manageable weight but still have internal support from impact. The spongy bone is kind of like those dried noodle cakes that you have in instant noodles!
Both compact and spongy bone have the rings of bone tissue with osteocytes and canaluci, the compact bone blood supply is in the middle, and the spongy bone is surrounded by blood.
46191-19600100Epiphysis – the ends of a long bone, edges of compact bone and the centre in spongy bone. This is the classic organisation of bone tissue.
Epiphyseal plate – this is made of cartilage in kids and is what allows bones to grow.
Diaphysis – the shaft of a long bone, has a cavity that is filled with bone marrow – red from making blood cells, and yellow in adults that stores fat mostly.
Bones are HIGHLY vascular – lots and lots of blood!!
Joins the broken ends of the bone together
Woven immature bone (bone tissue without the structure of compact bone) replaces the cartilage
Woven, immature bone becomes mature structured compact bone with is designed to withstand the forces of the bone.
Holds the bones in the right place for repair – provides some support
Bone is stronger than cartilage but still weak (the bone is not continuous yet)
Restores the function and structure from before the bone was broken.

Remodelling uses osteoblasts and clasts to remove older bone and replace with new bone. This process happens all the time anyway, in repair, it is breaking down WOVEN IMMATURE BONE and replacing it with NEW COMPACT BONE, thus restoring normal structure and function.

Bone is constantly being remodelling – this is when the osteoclasts reabsorb bone and osteoblasts make new bone. In this image, the black osteons are older and some have been absorbed by osteoclasts, with osteoblasts making the newer bone where the old bone has been removed.
The black osteons would be older osteons. The blue and red ones would be newer, and the green one would be the newest – they are often overlapping to make them stronger!
This remodelling can occur for lots of reasons. Some examples are:
When you get heavier, the bones experience more stress and so build denser bones that are better designed to hold your weight
When you get lighter, the bone doesn’t need to be as dense!
If you have extra calcium, your body can make MORE bones and your osetoblasts increase in activity to store the extra calcium away as bones

If you lack calcium in your blood, your osteoclasts can break down bones to release the calcium from the bone into the blood to get it back up to normal for other parts of your body to use it (your brain, heart and your muscles need calcium to work properly!)
If you are lifting weights for example, that places stress on the body – the muscles get bigger to better lift the weight, and the bones remodel to better support the weights.
The opposite occurs if you stop lifting weights – the body is a “use it or lose it” kind of machine – it only does what it HAS to.
Adults vs kids bones – the bones of children are more immature – the ends are still flexible and cartilaginous to allow for growth!

This course will lay the foundations of scientific knowledge required for future nursing practice including the basic structure, concepts and principles that underpin functioning of the human body.
The purpose of this course is to continue the development of the scientific knowledge required for future nursing practice.
The purpose of this course is to examine and apply Maatai Oranga (Health Science) in relation to Tikanga aa-Tapuhi.
On successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
LO1 : Explain the structure and function of a range of human body systems to support safe nursing practice.
LO2 : Analyse the principles of homeostasis in maintaining physiological balance relevant to nursing care.
LO3 : Describe the support, coordination and control of movement in the human body within a nursing context.
LO4 : Apply knowledge of human genetics and inheritance to nursing assessment and care planning.
LO5 : Demonstrate knowledge of the regulatory and integrative functions of the human body including sensory functions, to underpin nursing practice.

Much of the heart is cardiac muscle (myocardium). Unlike the skeletal muscle cells, cardiac muscle cells generate their own electrical impulses and conduct these impulses (action potentials) to the entire myocardium. These do not occur over the entire heart simultaneously; instead, different parts of the heart are depolarised to different extents at any instant in time. This causes small electric currents to flow in the extracellular fluid from one part of the body to another. These currents can be detected by placing sensitive electrodes on certain parts of the body. A recording of these currents forms an electrocardiogram (ECG).
By convention, the pairs of electrodes are placed in a certain order to give a series of ECG readings. Three of these are shown below.
Any potential difference (voltage) between each pair of electrodes will be amplified and then recorded by an electrocardiograph machine, as a series of up-and-down waves called deflection waves.

One of the most common tests carried out to estimate aspects of respiratory function is the peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) which measures the maximum rate of air flow out of the lungs. Peak flow rate will be reduced when there is any obstruction to air flow such as bronchoconstriction or inflammation caused by asthma or bronchitis. A simple peak flow meter can be used by patients at home to monitor their respiratory function day to day.

Joint surfaces, fitting perfectly into one another, are covered in hyaline cartilage to absorb shock and make movement smooth and painless. Synovial fluid lubricates the hyaline cartilage to facilitate frictionless movement.

A lever consists of a rigid arm, which is free to turn about a fixed point called the fulcrum. The fulcrum is a pivot point.
Components of a lever system – in this case a first-class lever system with the fulcrum in the middle.

Use a pencil as a fulcrum, a ruler as a lever and an eraser as the load. Effort will be provided by your finger to demonstrate how moving the fulcrum closer to or further away from the load effects the force needed to move the load. Do you agree with the following conclusion? Explain.
The closer the fulcrum to the load, the less force needed to lift the load. The closer the fulcrum to the force, the greater the force needed to lift the load.
Levers are divided into three types, or classes, according to the way the load and force arms are arranged around the fulcrum.

In a first-class lever, the FULCRUM (PIVOT) is in the Middle (see image above). When the fulcrum is midway between the force and the load, there is no change in force, speed or distance. If the fulcrum is closer to the load, big mechanical advantage is obtained.
Select and mark the first-class levers from the examples below: The question to ask is: WHAT IS IN THE MIDDLE? First class, look for the ones with the FULCRUM in the middle.
In the second-class lever, the load arm lies between the fulcrum and the force arm. In other words, the LOAD is in the middle.
The fulcrum is usually closer to the load, which reduces the force needed to accomplish the work.
A wheelbarrow can be seen as a second-class lever. List some other examples of the second-class lever:

In this class of levers, the EFFORT lies between the fulcrum and the load. Because of this a relatively large force is required to move the load. This is offset by the fact that it is possible to produce movement of the load over a long distance with a relatively small movement of the force arm. In a third-class lever there is usually a loss in force needed to accomplish the work, but a gain in speed or distance. When a cricket bat or golf club is swung, a third-class lever system acts.

The elbow acts as a fulcrum in both cases and the hands provide the force (hence the lower arm becomes part of the lever). The load (i.e. the puck or the ball) is moved at the end of the stick or bat.

The nervous system is one of the two major control systems of the human body (what is the other?). It consists of the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (spinal and cranial nerves).

The functioning of the nervous system can be divided into three parts:
Sensory function - the detection of changes in the internal and external environment.
Integrative function - the interpretation and decision-making functions.
Motor function - the initiation of actions in response to these changes e.g. muscular contraction or glandular secretions.

Jack and Jill have blood pressure issues. Jack has high blood pressure, and has been talking quinapril for about 1 year, and their GP has just added metoprolol to their prescription. Jack has been told they may need to be mindful of standing too quickly, as Jack might get a bit dizzy or even pass out; something called postural hypotension. Jack is really mindful, as their Dad had to get an angiogram, and then a bypass in a coronary vessel due to blocked coronary vessels and angina. Jill, on the other hand, has been having dizzy spells, and excessive thirst. They were admitted to hospital, and vitals were taken showing a bp of 80/55, with concentrated, low volume urine being noted by the admitting nurse. As a student nurse, you’ll need a robust understanding of how the cardiovascular system works, to understand what is happening for each of these people.
What determines blood pressure? You’ll need to think about our physiology as well as those factors that can change our blood pressure.
High blood pressure is defined as?
High blood pressure has several chronic, downstream consequences. What are they? Thinking about the implications for long term health and wellness, as well as why we care as nurses!
Low blood pressure has several acute consequences. These are?

You have nervous system processes that help to keep your blood pressure steady at rest, and help to increase or decrease it back to normal for exercise or after exercise, based on feedback from your body. We are going to focus on regulation – how your body RETURNS blood pressure to normal after it has been changed.

How does the nervous system detect and return blood pressure to normal when it is lower than normal (e.g. you’ve just stood up quickly and BP to your brain drops; think gravity – as for Jack’s postural hypotension)
How is this process different when it is higher than normal (e.g. after a run, after a fright, etc)
You also have renal system processes that use hormones to help return low blood pressure to normal over the long term.
The kidneys normally help to increase blood pressure if it is too low – this is a slower process (which takes minutes to hours, depending on the circumstances). Explain how this occurs.

The human body has what is called set points – this is where the body maintains homeostasis to, what your body thinks is normal. These set points will be slightly different between people. Sometimes, if your body has something that is constantly outside the normal range (e.g. if your BP is always high), your body changes its set point (it kind of goes, ahh fine, this is what normal is now) to your new normal. This is similar to when people from Dunedin laugh when Aucklanders say it’s cold, and they’re like, THIS ISNT COLD UNTIL YOUR TOILET IS FROZEN, GET IN THE BIN YOU WUSS. These two individuals have different ‘set points’ about what is cold.
What are Jack’s medications trying to do? Explain in plain, easy to understand language! Relate it back to the processes you described in question 6 and 7!
Why are medications for high blood pressure started when there are no symptoms of damage?

Atherosclerosis is the process by which blood vessels can become narrowed, because a fatty plaque builds up in the blood vessel. This narrowing can prevent blood flowing though the vessel, and even end up blocking the vessel. If this happens in the coronary vessels, this can cause angina, chest pain, or worse!
Where does the fatty deposit build up?
What does narrowing a blood vessel and preventing/restriction blood flow cause? What are some examples of these around the body?

Larry has been recently diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes mellitus, an endocrine disorder, after what appears to be many years of uncontrolled hyperglycaemia. He must measure his blood sugar every as he works with his diabetes nurse to bring it under control, and he will also need to have insulin injections and other medications to help his blood glucose regulation. Larry is a little overwhelmed, and isn’t sure of what this insulin is for. As his nurse, you need a robust understanding of what insulin does in the body a

Diabetes mellitus is a disease that involves the dysfunction of insulin and glucose regulation. There are two types, type 1 where the body fails to make insulin, and type 2 where the body is unable to respond to insulin when it is secreted.
*Where in the body, SPECIFICALLY, is insulin made?
*What hormone (or hormones!) acts in opposition to insulin, and where is it/they made?
*Explain what insulin does at a cellular level (you’ll need to think about how it travels in the body, what is binds to, and what happens)
*Insulin’s role in the fat tissue is:
What other molecules also influence blood glucose levels?

Insulin resistance is cause by excessively high blood sugar levels, which causes the body’s normal BLG set point to change (much like the blood pressure example earlier). Insulin is designed to only be high after a meal, so in normal function it shows a pattern like the accompanying diagram. When blood sugar is high LOTS, insulin will be high lots, and this signal loses meaning (kind of like if someone screamed, you’d pay attention, but if they were always screaming, you’d probably ignore them, because the scream is not an important signal anymore. Think about when woo girls scream, we aren’t going to check on them, they’re fine).
Yes I know it’s from Wikipedia, but it’s a great image and it’s available for common use and it was published.
Can you describe the normal BGL over the day? What about insulin?
In normal blood sugar regulation, does BGL go above the normal range?
What happens overnight? What could that mean for the morning?

When the body cells are resistant to the insulin signal, the pancreas tries to compensate by making MORE insulin, to make the signal meaningful again. Due to all this pancreas hyperactivity, damage and loss of function can occur, which means the pancreas now struggles to make enough insulin.
What would happen in the body now? How might we need to intervene?

Jack and Jill have blood pressure issues. Jack has high blood pressure, and has been talking quinapril for about 1 year, and their GP has just added metoprolol to their prescription. Jack has been told they may need to be mindful of standing too quickly, as Jack might get a bit dizzy or even pass out; something called postural hypotension. Jack is really mindful, as their Dad had to get an angiogram, and then a bypass in a coronary vessel due to blocked coronary vessels and angina. Jill, on the other hand, has been having dizzy spells, and excessive thirst. They were admitted to hospital, and vitals were taken showing a bp of 80/55, with concentrated, low volume urine being noted by the admitting nurse. As a student nurse, you’ll need a robust understanding of how the cardiovascular system works, to understand what is happening for each of these people.
What determines blood pressure? You’ll need to think about our physiology as well as those factors that can change our blood pressure.
High blood pressure is defined as?
High blood pressure has several chronic, downstream consequences. What are they? Thinking about the implications for long term health and wellness, as well as why we care as nurses!
Low blood pressure has several acute consequences. These are?

You have nervous system processes that help to keep your blood pressure steady at rest, and help to increase or decrease it back to normal for exercise or after exercise, based on feedback from your body. We are going to focus on regulation – how your body RETURNS blood pressure to normal after it has been changed.

How does the nervous system detect and return blood pressure to normal when it is lower than normal (e.g. you’ve just stood up quickly and BP to your brain drops; think gravity – as for Jack’s postural hypotension)
How is this process different when it is higher than normal (e.g. after a run, after a fright, etc)
You also have renal system processes that use hormones to help return low blood pressure to normal over the long term.
The kidneys normally help to increase blood pressure if it is too low – this is a slower process (which takes minutes to hours, depending on the circumstances). Explain how this occurs.

The human body has what is called set points – this is where the body maintains homeostasis to, what your body thinks is normal. These set points will be slightly different between people. Sometimes, if your body has something that is constantly outside the normal range (e.g. if your BP is always high), your body changes its set point (it kind of goes, ahh fine, this is what normal is now) to your new normal. This is similar to when people from Dunedin laugh when Aucklanders say it’s cold, and they’re like, THIS ISNT COLD UNTIL YOUR TOILET IS FROZEN, GET IN THE BIN YOU WUSS. These two individuals have different ‘set points’ about what is cold.
What are Jack’s medications trying to do? Explain in plain, easy to understand language! Relate it back to the processes you described in question 6 and 7!
Why are medications for high blood pressure started when there are no symptoms of damage?

Atherosclerosis is the process by which blood vessels can become narrowed, because a fatty plaque builds up in the blood vessel. Cardiac cycle | Patton: FIGURE 28-19 | The cardiac cycle. | Atrial systole. | Contraction (systole) of the atrial musculature. | Creates a pressure gradient that pushes blood out of the atria into the relaxed ventricles where the pressure is lower. | Isovolumetric ventricular contraction. | During the brief period of isovolumetric ventricular contraction, the intraventricular pressure begins to increase. close the atrioventricular valves—producing the first heart sound—but not enough to overcome arterial pressure and open the semilunar valves. This phase occurs between the start of ventricular systole and the opening of the semilunar valves, during which ventricular volume remains constant as the pressure increases rapidly. | Ejection. | The semilunar valves open and blood is ejected from the heart when the pressure in the ventricles exceeds the pressure in the pulmonary artery and aorta. An initial, shorter phase, called rapid ejection , is characterized by a marked increase in ventricular and aortic pressure and in aortic blood flow. The T wave of the ECG appears during the later, longer phase of reduced ejection (characterized by a less abrupt decrease in ventricular volume). A considerable quantity of blood, called the residual volume, normally remains in the ventricles at the end of the ejection period. In heart failure the residual volume remaining in the ventricles may greatly exceed that ejected during systole. | Isovolumetric ventricular relaxation. | Ventricular diastole, or relaxation, begins with the isovolumetric ventricular relaxation period of the cardiac cycle. It is the period between closure of the semilunar valves and opening of the atrioventricular valves. At the end of ventricular ejection, the semilunar valves close when the ventricular pressure drops below arterial pressure and pushes the valve flaps closed. As the valves snap shut, they produce the second heart sound. Closure of the semilunar valves prevents blood from re-entering the ventricular chambers from the pulmonary trunk and aorta. Both sets of valves are closed, and the ventricles are relaxing. | Ventricular relaxation causes a dramatic fall in intraventricular pressure but not enough to open the atrioventricular valves. Because the valves are closed, there is no change in volume. The atrioventricular valves do not open until the pressure in the atrial chambers increases above that in the relaxing ventricles. | Passive ventricular filling. | As the ventricles continue to relax, the intraventricular pressure continues to drop. That, along with rising | intraatrial | pressure produced by return of venous blood, produces a pressure gradient sufficient to force open the atrioventricular valves. Blood then rushes into the relaxing ventricles. | The rapid influx of blood into the ventricles lasts about 0.1 second and results in a dramatic increase in ventricular volume. The term diastasis is often used to describe a later, longer period of slow ventricular filling as ventricular diastole ends. The abrupt inflow of blood that occurred immediately after opening of the atrioventricular valves is followed by a slow but continuous flow of venous blood into the atria and then through the open atrioventricular valves into the ventricles. It is important to know what your textbook has to offer. Reading a textbook is a lot different than reading a novel. Active reading requires you to think critically – decide for example which information is important or not. The goal of active reading is to enhance your own knowledge and help you do well.

The Marieb text is a great resource for knowledge, to answer questions and to explore relationships between ideas and to apply this knowledge. This is different to being a passive reader who assumes the book will magically “teach” them everything they need to know to pass! An active reader knows that it is their job to get the information from the book and into their head.
This assignment is designed to help you familiarize yourself with the text so that you can use it efficiently and effectively.

To lay the foundation for scientific knowledge required for future nursing practice including the basic structure, concepts and principles that inderpin functioning of the human body.
### Nga Hua o te Ako | Learning Outcomes (LO)
On successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
* LO1: Explain the structure and function of a range of human body systems to support safe nursing practice.
* LO2: Analyse the principles of homeostasis in maintaining physiological balance relevant to nursing care.
* LO3 Describe the support, coordination and control of movement in the human body within a nursing context.
* LO4 Apply knowledge of human genetics and inheritance to nursing assessment and care planning.
* LO5 Demonstrate knowledge of the regulatory and integrative functions of the human body including sensory functions, to underpin nursing practice.

### Being an Active and Responsible Learner
Academic integrity means doing the right thing — being honest and fair in your studies. Always submit your own work, cite your sources, and follow ethical study practices.

Plagiarism means using someone else’s words or ideas without giving credit. This includes copying text, rewording someone’s ideas, or submitting another person’s work. Always reference your sources, including your own work from other courses. Written work may be checked with [Turnitin](http://www.turnitin.com/) to confirm originality.
Contract cheating means submitting work that isn’t your own — for example, getting someone else to do your assignment or using AI tools such as ChatGPT or Copilot to create work for you.

Assignments are designed to build your own skills. You can use AI tools to support your learning if stated in your course or assessment instructions. When permitted, you must acknowledge them properly and make sure they do not replace your own work.

At MIT, actions such as plagiarism and contract cheating are taken seriously, as they affect the credibility of everyone in our learning community. Learn more on the [Academic Integrity](https://www.manukau.ac.nz/student-life/current-students/student-support/academic-integrity) page of the MIT website.
Staying engaged and sharing your voice is also part of being an active learner.

To understand pathology (disease), we must first understand the normal structure and function of the body. This is what this semester is all about. The image on the right shows the flaps of the valves inside the heart. It also shows the cords that hold them and prevent them from opening to the wrong side. Dysfunction of these flaps and cords, may make it harder for the heart muscle to pump the blood to where it needs to go. All this hard work may make the heart chamber grow bigger in an effort to provide enough blood for bodily functions, a condition known as _"hypertrophy"_. ### What is the Literacy and Numeracy Assessment Tool for Adults?

The Literacy and Numeracy Tool for Adults is an online tool that helps lecturers design their teaching to support you. All ākonga studying at Levels 1 and 2 (and some ākonga at Level 3) do the assessment countrywide. **It is an online assessment that you cannot fail. **

You do the assessment twice during your course, once at the beginning, then again at the end. Doing it twice shows you how much you have improved during your study. It also helps your lecturer to be sure that their teaching is helping you.

Literacy means reading and writing skills. Things like reading the instructions for a test, or filling out forms like your MIT enrolment form. Numeracy means how good you are with day-to-day numbers. Things like working out how much money you have to spend on kai at the cafeteria.

Strong literacy and numeracy skills will help you to succeed in school, work, and daily living. Doing the assessments will show you where the gaps are in your knowledge and where together we can help you improve your skills.
If you need help in a specific area, we have some fun exercises and a cool website for you to play some learning games - links are below.
### What do I need to do?

You will receive your unique code from the kaiako (lecturer), log into the computer, and start the assessment. An assessment takes about an hour for the reading and an hour for the numeracy assessment. The good news is that you don’t have to do it all at once, you can log back on the site and finish it later.
Your kaiako will give you enough time to finish the assessments.

In short, misconduct is when you do not play by the rules. You gain an unfair advantage by using resources or help that is not permitted. In HS2 that may mean using someone or something else to help you with an assessment or to do it for you. This includes another local or remote person, AI or an internet search. It also means having unpermitted resources with you while doing the assessment and using them.

It is tragic that a lot of time and effort have to go into it to make sure that students play by the rules. Every semester student test and exam are investigated to try to ensure adherence to the rules. The reason: **TO PROTECT THE INTEGRITY OF YOUR QUALIFICATIONS.** If cheating becomes common, your qualifications become worthless.
Misconduct during assessments is defined as any attempt by a student to gain an unfair advantage in a summative assessment.
It includes, but is not limited to, the student:
* Copying information directly from another student (current or past), either in whole or in part, with or without their consent;
* Allowing another student to copy their summative assessment (in part or whole);
* Facilitating the electronic transfer, or giving soft copies, of their assessment work to other students;
* Giving or lending a printed or hand-written copy of their assessment to another student;
* Failing to exercise reasonable care and responsibility in protecting their work from being accessed by other students. This includes giving someone the opportunity to copy their work;
Using or having access to prohibited resources or reference material, written or electronic, in a test or examination;
* Communicating with another student in a test/examination to transfer information by way of electronic, voice, visual or other means;
* Accessing or taking test or examination question papers without approval;
* Failing to follow the invigilator’s instructions;
* Plagiarism (i.e. using the work of another without indicating that the ideas are not their own).
* Presenting someone else’s work as one’s own for summative assessment;
* Any action that is aimed to defeat the purpose of the summative assessment;
* Breaching any rule or regulation relating to summative assessment;
* Academic or research practices that bring or are likely to bring MIT into disrepute; and
* Misrepresenting a disability, temporary illness or injury, or exceptional circumstances beyond one’s control and then seeking special conditions or an aegrotat pass.

Written work for this programme/course may be submitted to Turnitin for originality checking to help detect academic misconduct. Turnitin is an originality checking and plagiarism prevention service, operated by a third party called iParadigms, which Manukau Institute of Technology Limited (MIT) is licensed to use.

Where Turnitin is used, students must submit their work for assessment to the Canvas learning management system, so Turnitin may analyse similarity to other work published on the Internet (which includes the Turnitin student assignment submission repository). MIT staff and students can view the Turnitin report from this submission, which may be used to assist learners with improving their academic writing. Where appropriate, the Turnitin similarity data may be used in an academic integrity investigation (more information available in the Student Regulations).

Student access to Turnitin is on the terms stipulated in the agreement between the student and Turnitin. Work submitted to Canvas (where Turnitin is embedded) may be retained as part of the Turnitin database for ongoing comparison with other work submitted. By enrolling on this course/programme, students agree to their work being submitted to Turnitin on the terms and conditions outlined on the Turnitin website. Declining to use Turnitin could result in a student being unable to complete a course or programme. For further information about Turnitin and the terms and conditions of use, please refer to the Turnitin website at [www.turnitin.com](http://www.turnitin.com).

### Understanding Academic Integrity with AI and Third-Party Tools

Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, such as ChatGPT or Copilot, use generative technology to create text or ideas based on prompts you give them. These tools can be great for exploring ideas or practising skills.
However, when it comes to assessments, you should only use AI **if your course or assessment instructions say you can**. Always check your instructions carefully and ask your kaiako if you’re unsure.
You may use AI tools only if your kaiako or assessment instructions say so.
If allowed, you must clearly explain:
* Which AI system you used (for example, ChatGPT, Copilot, DALL·E)
* How you used it (for example, to generate ideas, outlines, or examples)
* Where in your work the AI contributed
_I acknowledge the use of ChatGPT to draft ideas for Section 2 of my report. The prompts used included: [insert prompts]. The text was reviewed and rewritten in my own words._ |
You must **not** use AI tools to:
* Write or edit parts of your assessment
* Create images, code, or text for graded tasks
* Generate answers or complete exams or tests
If you do, it may be considered [academic misconduct,](https://www.manukau.ac.nz/student-life/current-students/student-support/academic-integrity/) which can result in:
If AI use isn’t mentioned, it’s best not to use it — just check first.
If you're stressed about completing an assignment, don't risk misconduct. Get help from legitimate sources:
DON’T try to get help from:
• Students who have already taken the class
• Family members or friends who offer to do your work
• Using an online writing tool such as ChatGPT to answer your assessment questions

If you get help from other students, family, friends, or companies that do your work for you, this is cheating. What could happen if you are caught cheating? Getting a lower mark, or a 0 on your assignment, failing your course, or having to leave MIT.
The best way to succeed is to check with your kaiako and use our [MIT support services](https://www.manukau.ac.nz/student-life/current-students/student-support/).

722.541 Health Science 2 is a 15 point BN2 paper which contains Anatomy, Physiology and Bioscience content. This course has 722.539 Health Science 1 as a prerequisite.

HS2 has both a theory and a practical component. You must score 50% or more total weighted mark to achieve a pass in this course, and you must met the standard for laboratory attendance. HS2 has 2 types of summative assessment; continuous tests through the semester worth a total of 50% all together and a final exam worth 50% that assesses all the modules covered in HS2.

Weekly on campus lecture times for HS2 are communicated on Canvas calender, the MIT online timetable and the wall flowers. In the case that a student misses a lecture (including when they are on clinical placements) it is expected that the student will catch up on that lecture using the materials available on CANVAS.

[Semester Timetable](https://canvas.manukau.ac.nz/courses/61986/pages/semester-timetable "Semester Timetable")**[](https://canvas.manukau.ac.nz/courses/61986/pages/semester-timetable "Semester Timetable")** for chapter links as well as all the timetable issues listed above.
Last semester you started your science journey and should be very familiar with the following aspects:
* Demonstrate using the Textbook index, glossary and prefixes and suffixes to find the location and meaning of words
* Understand and demonstrate the use of directional terms
* Explain the major cavities of the human body and their subdivisions
* Describe the levels of organisation of the human body

It is expected that you know these terms as these will be put to good use over your second semester. It may be a good opportunity to consider the PQ4R method and the 10-24-7 idea to help you review your work regularly.

Remember your text book is an extremely useful tool. Just like learning to use a power tool or a new TV etc, you need to know how to use your text book. Take some time to review the following exercise ["Making friends with my text book"](https://canvas.manukau.ac.nz/courses/61986/files/8820238/download?verifier=SsRE4uTJtg9tBjwQV64Wr6Kylq7W8Halx2HE1Aqb "Making friends with the text.docx") and become familiar with this book. Although this text is written by two people, you will find most lecturers refer fondly to the text as Patton (just remember for APA referencing you will need to refer to both authors).

Studying Anatomy and Physiology is like looking at an iceberg - we just sort of cover the "tip" in class - the bit of the iceberg you can see...underneath that is the biggest part which we cannot see. You need to do more "unseen" work to really have a good understanding of how everything works, and everything you need to know is in this book! At the very least, please read the Chapter Summary for the upcoming work before attending the lectures. After the lectures, you can hone in on particular areas that you need to work on by processing those sections of the text in more depth.

Remember! A lot of what you studied in HS1 are foundational for HS2, so don't forget all that knowledge you have gained! It's a good idea to go back and review Module 1 - cells, tissue and body system are important to build upon!

When writing notes, these tips may be useful:
* write for yourself, and write every day
* be informal, using language you are comfortable with
* write by hand if you prefer
* write in your own language where appropriate (though remember you might need to use technical terms in English!)
* try sitting in different places and positions
* record not just events but reflection on process and your interpretations
* connect personal and professional experiences to concepts and theories.
Using reflective practice when it comes to your notes might be useful too!
#### Keeping a reflective journal can help you to
* focus your thoughts and develop your ideas
* develop your voice and gain confidence
* experiment with ideas and ask questions
* organise your thinking through exploring and mapping complex issues
* develop your conceptual and analytical skills
* reflect upon and make sense of experiences and the processes behind them
* express your feelings and emotional responses
* become aware of your actions and strategies
* develop your writing style and skills, and explore different styles of writing
**Study tips: How to Tackle Multiple Choice Questions**
This link here also goes into detail about tackling MCQ's - have a look!
Some of the detail from this page:

... Preview the whole test before beginning to answer any questions. Make sure your copy has no missing or duplicate pages. Read the directions carefully. **Start with questions you can readily answer...

**... to build your confidence and to save time for the harder ones. When you identify a correct response carefully mark this on the question paper. If you are unable to make a choice and need to spend more time with the question, or you answered the question but are not at all sure that you made the correct choice, put a big question mark beside that question, and move on to the next. Avoid getting bogged down on one question part of the way through the exam. It is much better to move on and finish all of those questions that you can answer and then to come back later to process the problematic questions. Sometimes the answer will occur to you simply because you are more relaxed after having answered other questions. **Plan your time and pace yourself

** ... Allocate your time. For most cases, you want to spend 1-2 minutes only on a question. If you cannot answer a question within this time, skip it and come back to it later. Set progress points at the beginning of the test and use them to monitor your progress, such as, know what question you should be answering at the 30-minute mark. **Allocate time to review your answers...

** ... and to transfer your answers to the computer sheet. It is best to transfer all responses to the answer sheet at the same time once you have answered all questions on your question paper (thus reducing the probability of making a mistake). Note however that you will not be given additional time at the end of the test to transfer your answers. **Read each question carefully **
... Multiple-choice tests also examine your ability to read carefully and thoughtfully, as much as they test your ability to recall and reason.
** Circle or underline key words, such as "all," "always," "never," "none," "not," "few," "many," some," and "sometimes."

** Identifying what lecture, reading, or laboratory exercise the question is from might help you narrow the choice of possible responses. (On many tests the questions are scrambled and do not follow the order that topics were presented in lectures or labs.)
** Answer each question as the professor intended, that is, within the context of the course material that was taught.
** Some students find it helpful to read the question and try to recall the answer from memory before looking at each of the five responses.
** Identify if the question is looking for a true or false statement. Then label each of the five responses as "true" or "false" and eliminate those that do not correctly complete the question.
**... and don't just stop when you come upon the one that seems likely.
* Don't select a response just because you remember learning the information in the course; it may be a "true" statement in its own right, but not the correct answer to the question.
* Don't dismiss a response because it seems too obvious and simple an answer; if you are well prepared for the test, some of the questions may appear very straight forward.
* Don't be persuaded by fancy terms in the question; don't say to yourself, "That sounds impressive, so it must be the right answer."
* As you read through the possible responses, mark off the ones you know are wrong. This will save time if you have to come back to the question later.

**... Change answers only if you have a good reason for doing so. (Changing your answer from response "b" because you selected "b" to the previous two questions is not a good reason.) The origin of the myth that students most often change correct answers to wrong answers is probably that it is the wrong answers that students remember most when reviewing the test (for you are less likely to remember the answers you changed from "wrong" to "right"). **If two responses appear to be equally correct... **

... eliminate the response that appears to be least related to the question being asked. Remember, you are looking for the best answer, not only a correct one. Some responses may be correct but are not directly related to the question. **If you are not certain of an answer, guess... **

... as there is no penalty for wrong answers. Eliminate the responses you know are incorrect. Narrow down your selection to two responses and then compare them and identify how they differ. Finally, make an informed guess.

Due to the NZ Health & Safety act (2015) it is a **compulsory requirement** that every student **at****each new semester** completes this online Laboratory Health & Safety Orientation. This orientation must be completed before you will be permitted to undertake any practical work in the laboratories. Your safety and the safety of our staff is of paramount concern to MIT.
1. Watch the video using the link below
2. Complete the quiz to gain 100% pass (this may be attempted multiple times)
3. Your lecturer will mark you off as having participated and passed this orientation

Over the course of the semester you will have 6 laboratories, 2 for each module. This means you will have 6 labs over the semester (they are arranged to not clash with your clinical activities). The labs are | **MODULE 1** | **MODULE 2** | **MODULE 3**
1\. Lab 1: Cardiovascular System 2. Lab 2: Respiratory System | 3\. Lab 3: Musculoskeletal System 4\. Lab 4: Nervous System | 5\. Lab 5: Reproduction 6\. Lab 6: Special Senses
**There are online labs for all 6 labs. These are set up in quizzes,** and align to your lab book. These online labs are designed to:
* be used by all students to prepare for on-campus labs.
* help you to learn the content as you go through it.
* be used by students that miss a lab to catch up. An achievement of 50% in these quizzes is required if it is used for this purpose.
There will be other practice and attendance quizzes for you to do as well to check your understanding.

There is a requirement to attend your labs to be allowed to pass this course, which is 80% completion._Your lab attendance is entered into CANVAS so you can check this over the semester_. If there are any questions, you can contact your lecturer to get some help. If you haven't been marked off for a lab, please contact your lecturer to discuss getting this done.

**Complete your [Health and Safety quiz](https://canvas.manukau.ac.nz/courses/61986/assignments/268558 "NEW Year 1 & 2 Laboratory Health & Safety Orientation: COMPULSORY") and ensure that you attain 20/20 for it before coming to any labs. It must be done every semester. **

Blood vessels are the 'vascular' part of the Cardiovascular system. Blood vessels are found throughout the body and range in length and size, from the width of your index finger, to so small only a single red blood cell can wiggle through at a time. You'll already know about blood cells, so you'll appreciate just how small these vessels are! This important part of the circulatory system allows for blood to travel to every single cell in the body (through _tissue perfusion_), where the blood will deliver oxygen and nutrients to all the cells of the body, and receive waste products to be removed from the body.

**BLOOD VESSELS** Why would you as nursing students and eventually nurses have to learn about the structure and function of blood vessels. Think about: 1\. nursing procedures involving blood vessels: drawing blood, inserting an IV, what else? ; 2\. vital signs: measuring blood pressure, taking pulse, capillary refill (e.g. in burn wounds), describing skin colour and temperature,what else?; 3\. diseases involving blood vessels (e.g. atherosclerosis, stroke, DVT), what else?; 4\. Infection control, etc. I asked copilot to create me a word cloud about nurses using knowledge about blood vessels. It came up with the image on the right. Think about the aspects highlighted in it. ![dec34c1c-ee13-4132-9f4e-1426d5240746.jpg](https://canvas.manukau.ac.nz/courses/61986/files/8933723/preview?verifier=UIULNf94IWEFVb5SBICcXrGHOvaJYtKDN1LVh7OB) |
Humans have a **closed** blood system. Blood is circulated around and around in a loop and used over and over. Humans further have a **double** circulation.
* In the **pulmonary circulation** deoxygenated blood is sent from the right half of the heart tot lungs to be oxygenated. It returns as oxygenated blood to the left side of the heart.
* In the **systemic circulation** oxygenated blood is sent to the body by the left side of the hear and returns as deoxygenated blood to the right side of the heart.
Basically we have three kinds of blood vessels:
* Those taking blood away from the heart = **arteries**
* Those bringing blood to the heart =**veins**
* Those connecting the arteries and the veins **= capillaries.** The branching vessels form **capillary beds** \- sites for exchange.** **

![blood vessels cvs1](https://canvas.manukau.ac.nz/courses/61986/files/8819893/download?verifier=k0yG5svEoFoGes3M2ngIrgL2ERyJIlUNh5gZ4sEr&wrap=1) | **Blood vessels under the microscope.** ![BLOOD VESSELS LETTERED.JPEG](https://canvas.manukau.ac.nz/courses/61986/files/8931585/preview?verifier=VKSAQ0Eu4Nu3F2PVSFVM212YVwrGjVey05Nf9LsH) B and E in the images above are the lumens of the two blood vessels with some blood in it. Look at the higher magnifications below to see the red blood cells (erythrocytes).
**ARTERIES** **The letters refer to the first micrograph.**
* High pressure blood vessels that must withstand the force of the blood pumped into it by the powerful contraction of the heart.
* Bleeding from an artery would pulse. Pulses are also felt in arteries wher they cross bones. No pulsation is felt in veins.

* Arteries are built to resist this pulsing force by having elastic layers - the **internal (G)** and **external elastic laminae** (H) as well as a **thick smooth muscle layer** , the **tunica media****(A)****.**
* You must be able to identify an artery in a micrograph like the one below:

Can you see the black zig zag layer? That is the **internal elastic lamina**. When the heart pushes blood into the artery, it straightens out, and when the heart relaxes, it recoils into the the zig-zag shape. It is part of the **tunica intima (G),** the inner layer of the blood vessel. (Damage to the endothelial part (e.g. by hypertension, smoking, high blood sugar levels, etc.) of the tunica intima leads to atherosclerosis, the buildup of plaque in the blood vessels which is responsible for many cardiovascular problems). |
* Deep of the tunica interna, we find the **smooth muscle layer** , the**tunica media (A).** You can see the spindle shaped cells in it if you look closely.

* There is a second black layer, the **external elastic lamina** which is part of a connective tissue layer, the adventitia, or **tunica externa (C)**. This layer connects the blood vessel to the surrounding tissues and supports it.
* An artery keeps its shape when it is empty because of the thick tunica media.

* The biggest arteries are the**aorta (** sending oxygenated blood from the **left ventricle** to the whole body including the heart) and the **pulmonary artery** (sending blood from the **right ventricle** to the lungs to be oxygenated
**VEINS** **The letters refer to the first micrograph.**
* Veins are low pressure blood vessels returning blood to the heart.
* Bleeding from a vein would flow smoothly. There is no pump action behind it. The capillary beds and the many valves smooth out the flow.
* Like the artery, veins also have an internal **tunica intima, a middle tunica media (D)** and an **external adventitia or tunica externa (F)**.
* For the size of the vessel, the two inner layers are**thinner** and the**tunica externa** **thicker** than the corresponding layers in an artery.
* We cannot distinguish an internal nor external elastic laminae in the vein.
* A vein **loses it shape** when it is empty because of the thinner tunica media.

* The biggest veins are the vena cava superior (collecting blood from the head and upper parts of the body) and the inferior vena cava (collecting blood from the legs and lower parts of the body and taking it to the right atrium
* Capillaries connect the arteries and the veins.

* They are the sites where **exchange processes** happen. Nutrient absorption, filtration in the kidneys, gaseous exchange in the lungs and tissues, waste and hormones are up and offloaded in capillary beds.
* For this purpose they are thin-walled - they only have a **tunica intima. **
* They are also extremely thin in diameter- so thin that in some of them red blood cells must fold or turn side-ways to get through them.
* Three main types of capillaries are found in the body - each suitable for the function that it must fulfil in the specific location where they are found.

* **Continuous capillaries**(with no holes) are found at places where a tight barrier are needed (like in the **blood brain barrier (BBB)**). Substances like very small particles (gases) and lipid soluble substances (like alcohol) can diffuse through and can also pass through the openings between the cells.

* **Fenestrated capillaries** (with small holes) are typically found in the filtration membrane in the glomerulus of the kidney where they must retain proteins and blood cells in the blood but must allow water, electrolytes, sugar, amino acids to filter through.
* **Discontinuous capillaries** (sinusoidal capillaries) have large openings in their walls so that blood cells and proteins can get through. Places where this kind of capillary are needed is like:
* The bone marrow, where blood cells must be able to get from their place of manufacturing (in the bone marrow) to their destination (the blood stream).
* The spleen, where red blood cells need to be taken out of the blood steam to be recycled.

| ![3-s2.0-B9780123944474400192-f40019-02-9780123944474 capillary.jpg](https://canvas.manukau.ac.nz/courses/61986/files/8931645/preview?verifier=gIWWuETA35T3MIU5B9iR3TtDRVXNvzSBJno1zHAp) A capillary in cross section. **EXCHANGE OVER A CAPILLARY ** **![CAP MOVEMENT 2108_Capillary_ExchangeN.jpg](https://canvas.manukau.ac.nz/courses/61986/files/8931647/preview?verifier=LAGZzwRHqtTbSBOtJmzYe4pIFp5mN18hwG8BLM5Q)**

* On the arterial side of the capillary bed the **hydrostatic pressure** is high due to the pumping force of the heart. This forces more fluid to leak out of the blood vessels into the interstitium than can return: leading to a net loss of fluid. It favours the process of **filtration. **
* In the middle of a capillary bed, there is no net outflow or inflow as hydrostatic pressure equals oncotic pressure.
* At the venous side the backflow exceeds the outflow and favours the process of **reabsorption**.

* This is so because of the high **oncotic pressure,** due to the high**** concentration of colloids, (such as proteins) in the blood vessel. Because of the prior outflow of fluid, the blood on the venous side is more "concentrated" drawing the fluid back in.

The heart is a muscular organ that functions to generate a pumping force. This pumping force (which is what generates the _hydrostatic force_ in the blood vessels) helps to push blood through vessels all around the body, allowing for _tissue perfusion _and delivering oxygen and nutrients to the cells. Without the heart, the cells of the body would receive no oxygen or nutrients, and toxic waste products would build up, as they would have no way to be removed from cells. The heart is extremely important for healthcare, as poor cardiovascular health is prevalent in NZ, and around the world; and has wide-ranging effects on the body.

#### **SAQ: Describe the chambers of the heart.(4)**
* The heart is divided into a left and right side, separated by a muscular septum (0.5).
* On each side there are two chambers, an upper and a lower one (0.5)
* The two upper chambers, the atria, (0.5) are thin walled (0.5)
* and send it through the Atrio Ventricular (AV)valves (0.5)
* to the lower thick walled chambers, the ventricles (0.5).
* The ventricles are the pumping chambers (0.5).
* They send blood to the lungs (R) and body (L) respectively(0.5).
#### **SAQ: What are the semilunar valves of the heart?(3)**
* The two semilunar valves each has three half moon shaped flaps (0.5) that prevent backflow of blood from the large arteries leaving the ventricles(0.5) .
* When they close, a DUB sound is typically heart (the second heart sound). (0.5)
* A semilunar valve, the pulmonary valve (0.5), prevents backflow of blood from the pulmonary artery to the right ventricle (0.5) .
* Another semilunar valve, the aortic valve( 0.5), prevents backflow of blood from the pulmonary artery to the left ventricle (0.5).

In the middle of the image below, you see the three semilunar flaps of the aortic valve. We can clearly see the ostea above the flaps telling us that this is the aortic valve and not the pulmonary valve. (The aorta is the large white vessel coming from the left ventricle and going to the body). ![image.png](https://canvas.manukau.ac.nz/courses/61986/files/8927085/preview?verifier=ObqLUyKubszm78070U3fIdNKhkDV7irXAIQPVqcp)** **
#### **SAQ: Describe the AV valves of the heart.(4)**
* The two AV valves each separates an atrium and a ventricle (0.5)
* on the right and left side of the heart (0.5).
* to the atria when the ventricles contract (0.5).
* When they close, a LUB sound is typically heart (the first heart sound).
* The tricuspid valve (on the right side) has 3 delicate flaps(0.5).
* The mitral (bicuspid) valve (on the left side) has 2 robust and large flaps (seen on image)(0.5).
* The valves can only open to the ventricular side (0.5)
* as their flaps are held back by chordae tendinea (0.5)
* attaching them to the papillary muscles to the ventricular wall (0.5).

Blood pressure is one of the most important physiological processes you'll learn about this year, and blood pressure changes are a risk factor in multiple different serious health conditions in the body. In NZ hypertension is increasingly prevalent, and found alongside diabetes, obesity and CVD. | **Blood pressure regulation** Blood pressure is regulated by:
**1.Neural mechanisms** (baroreceptors, chemoreceptors, autonomic nervous system) for rapid control.
**2.Hormonal mechanisms** (RAAS, ADH, aldosterone, ANP) for intermediate and long-term control.
**3.Renal mechanisms** (kidneys regulating fluid and salt balance) for long-term control.
4.**Blood vessels** and the **heart** act as the main **effectors** that ultimately increase or decrease blood pressure.

* * one **direct mechanism **altering the Glomerular filtration rate ; and
* one **indirect** mechanism (the RAAS) using a cascade of effects starting in our **kidneys (RAAS).**

* **CO = Cardiac Output** = blood ejected by heart per minute (increases with Stroke Volume and Heart Rate)
* **SV = Stroke Volume** = blood ejected by heart per beat (increases with high **blood volume,** more powerful **heart contractions** and increased **venous return (blood volume)) **
* **HR = Heart Rate** = beats per minute (increases with **exercise** and when stimulated by acceleratory centre in brain - sympathetic nervous impulses)

* **PR = Peripheral Resistance** = push back from blood vessels (increases when vessels are**longer** and **narrower** (constricted or blocked), or the blood is more **viscous** (e.g. syrupy with lots of sugar in it or more concentrated)
**Patton: FIGURE 30-2:** The primary principle of circulation.

_Fluid always travels from an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure. Fluid flows from an area of high pressure in the tank (100 mmHg) toward the area of low pressure above the bucket (0 mmHg). Blood likewise tends to move from an area of high pressure at the beginning of the aorta (100 mmHg) toward the area of lowest pressure at the end of the venae cavae (0 mmHg). Blood flow between any two points in the circulatory system can always be predicted by the pressure gradient._

Adequate blood pressure is needed to maintain adequate perfusion of all cells, but especially the cells of the vital organs such as the brain, the heart and the kidneys. It is then no surprise that our body is much better at increasing blood pressure than decreasing it. Chronic high hypertension often needs to be treated by using pharmacological interventions and lifestyles changes to bring this back into normal balance.

**MORE IMPORTANT CONCEPTS ABOUT FACTORS THAT AFFECT BLOOD PRESSURE BY AFFECTING THE HEART**
* **Inotropy** has to do with **force of contraction** of the myocardium. More forceful contractions increases CO.
* **Chronotropy** has to do with timing. Heart rate. Chemicals that have **positive chronotropic effects, increases heart rate** and therefor CO and BP.
**Epinephrine (adrenaline)** | Positive inotropic and positive chronotropic | Stimulates β₁-adrenergic receptors → ↑ heart rate and ↑ force of contraction
**Norepinephrine (noradrenaline)** | Positive inotropic (mild positive chronotropic) | Strong β₁ stimulation increases contractility; reflex bradycardia may limit HR increase
**Acetylcholine** | Negative chronotropic | Parasympathetic neurotransmitter → slows SA node firing and AV conduction
**Calcium channel blockers** | Negative inotropic (also negative chronotropic) | Reduce calcium entry into cardiac cells → ↓ contractility and ↓ heart rate
**Digoxin** | Positive inotropic | Increases intracellular calcium → stronger cardiac contraction
**Atropine** | Positive chronotropic | Blocks parasympathetic (vagal) input → ↑ heart rate
**Beta blockers** | Negative chronotropic (also negative inotropic) | Block sympathetic stimulation → ↓ heart rate and ↓ contractility

**Hypercalcemia (Ca 2+)** | Potentially life-threatening arrhythmias; Positive chrono- and inotropic. | **Accelerates heart contraction**(shortening the QT interval) and **increases cardiac contractility**
**Hypocalcemia (Ca 2+)******| May lead to congestive heart failure; Negative chrono and inotropic. | Reduce left ventricular contractility, resulting in **decreased SV** ; prolonged QT interval

**Hyperkalemia (K +)******| Potentially life-threatening arrhythmias; Slows down heart. Negative chronotropic | **Delays electrical signaling**(peaked T waves and widened QRS), making the heart weaker
**Hypokalemia (K +)** | Speeds up the heart; Positive chronotropic | Elevated risk of ventricular ectopy, fibrillation, and tachycardia due to increased automaticity
