Circulatory shock is when there is **inadequate blood flow to meet the needs of the tissue** , due to some kind of change impacting on blood flow around the body.

Shock is a serious event, and if missed, can lead to death. In fact, in the stages of shock, there comes a point where we are unable to reverse or treat the damage caused by shock, and someone in the latest stages of shock will die.
It is something that must be carefully monitored for, in many different cases for example:

* HYPOVOLEMIA: Any condition that may lead to fluid loss (e.g. blood, CSF, plasm, serum, gastrointestinal fluids)** including traumatic injury** and**burns** ,**dehydration** and**gastrointestinal conditions** (where diarree and or vomiting can lead to fluid loss),
* CARDIOGENIC: Any condition that**causes the heart to struggle to pump** the blood due to being injured/diseased/deprived of blood.
* OBSTRUCTIVE: flow to heart and/or from it is blocked e.g. by blood clots in the vessels to or from the lungs or body or the heart prevented from filling as in cardiac tamponade.
* DISTRIBUTIVE SHOCK \- conditions that lead to the fluid being in the wrong fluid compartment:

* SEPTIC & ANAPHYLACTIC: Any condition that **activates the immune response with histamine release** such as**infections** and severe **allergic reactions**. Histamine makes the blood vessels leaky so that fluids move out of the blood vessels into the i**nterstitial spaces** leaving the blood system with inadequate fluid to perfuse the whole body.

* NEUROGENIC: Any condition that leads to **massive vasodilation as in neurogenic shock** due to spinal injury above T6. Blood vessel diameter is maintained by a balance of stimulation from the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions of the autonomic nervous system. They are normally **slightly constricted** due to stronger sympathetic stimulation. If this sympathetic stimulation is disrupted, the blood vessels lose their **tone and dilate.** The blood vessel space becomes too large for the blood volume leading to fall in blood pressure. Also, with lack of sympathetic stimulation, the **heart rate drops**(bradycardia) so that Cardiac Output drops. (Besides an injury to the spinal cord or medulla, depressive drugs, emotional stress, or some other factor, may also make the blood vessels dilate significantly).
1. **Initial non-progressive phase**(Compensatory mechanisms to maintain the homeostasis). Patient has good chance of survival.
2. ###### **Progressive phase**(Failure of compensatory mechanisms). Patient can still be saved with expert interventions.
3. ###### **Irreversible stage**(Cellular injury and tissue injury is so severe that condition does not revert back to normal). Nothing further can be done.

The signs and symptoms of shock vary depending on the [type of shock](https://www-clinicalkey-com.ezproxy.manukau.ac.nz/student/nursing/content/book/3-s2.0-B9780729543910000326?origin=share&title=Understanding+Pathophysiology+Australia+and+New+Zealand+Edition&meta=2023%2C+Buckley%2C+Thomas&img=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.clinicalkey.com%2Fck-thumbnails%2FC20200021407%2Fcov200h.gif) and the [stage of shock.](https://www.histopathology.guru/stages-of-shock/)
A patient that is in shock is

* **usually pale, has a *cool and clammy (sticky) skin**(**vasoconstriction** causes low blood flow to the skin since blood is diverted away from the skin to the vital organs). (Exception: "**Warm shock"** with warm flushed skin due to vasodilation caused by fever can present if the patient goes into septic shock due to a bacterial infection);
* **a rapid heart rate**(the heart is stimulated by the **sympathetic nervous system** to restore blood flow);(Exception: "**Neurogenic shock"** with bradycardia due to loss of sympathetic tone);
* **is breathing fast and shallow**(breathing is stimulated by the**sympathetic nervous system** to try to get more oxygen in the body);
* **excessive sweating**(due to adrenaline released as result of **sympathetic nervous system activation.**
* **may be confused and/or anxious** (low levels of oxygen reach the brain), and
* 1\. not enough blood to perfuse the whole body (hypovolemic shock after fluid (blood-, serum-, CSF) -loss);
* 2\. heart cannot beat strong enough to get blood to whole body (cardiogenic shock);
* 3. obstructions prevent the heart from filling (obstructive shock);

* 4\. the blood is in the wrong fluid compartment (such as when many capillaries are dilated simultaneously as in neurogenic shock), blood vessels are leaky and fluid leaks out into the tissue (in anaphylactic and septic shock) due to the effects of histamine.
* **The progression of shock when positive feedback loops lead to further reductions in cardiac output.**

The severe decline in cardiac output leads to massive vasodilation, decreased blood volume (due to increased capillary permeability) and organ ischaemia. These cause further decline in cardiac output.

Table 23:13 from Maguire, (2023) gives a summary of the different types of shock, their causes, how the body tries to maintain homeostasis and some late signs and symptoms.
TYPE | CAUSE | COMPENSATORY PHYSIOLOGICAL ADAPTATIONS | LATE SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS

**Cardiogenic shock** | Myocardial dysfunction, tissue hypoxia | Heart rate ↑, preload ↑, stroke volume ↑, systemic and pulmonary oedema ↑ | ↓ mental status, dusky skin colour, hypotension, oliguria, dyspnoea

**Hypovolaemic shock** | Loss of fluid volume | Heart rate ↑, peripheral resistance ↑, cardiac output ↑, tissue perfusion ↑ (initially), water retention ↑ (initially) | Failed compensation and ↓ tissue perfusion, poor skin turgor, thirst, oliguria, low preload, tachycardia, thready pulse, ↓ mental status

**Neurogenic shock** | Trauma to spinal cord or medulla, Interrupted supply of oxygen or glucose to the medulla, depressive drugs, anaesthetic agents, severe emotional stress and pain | Interrupted sympathetic activity, relative hypovolaemia to vasodilation, peripheral vascular resistance ↓, tissue hypoperfusion | Bradycardia

**Anaphylactic shock** | Anaphylaxis | Vasodilation, peripheral pooling, hypovolaemia, tissue hypoperfusion | Sudden and progression to death within mins, anxiety, difficulty breathing, gastrointestinal cramps, oedema, hives, burning and itching of skin, ↓ blood pressure, ↓ mental status

**Septic shock** | Microorganism | Activated complement system and coagulation cascade, activated kinins, activated inflammatory response, widespread vasodilation, cardiac output ↑, myocardial contractility ↓, hypoperfusion, low peripheral vascular resistance, systemic oedema | Tachycardia, systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), low arterial pressure, temperature instability, deranged renal function, gastrointestinal mucosa changes that allow gut bacteria into the blood stream, jaundice, clotting abnormalities, deterioration of mental status, adult respiratory distress syndrome

[MODULE 1.1: Homeostatic Mechanisms: Regulation of Blood Pressure - THE BULLET POINTS](https://canvas.manukau.ac.nz/courses/61986/pages/module-1-dot-1-homeostatic-mechanisms-regulation-of-blood-pressure-the-bullet-points "MODULE 1.1: Homeostatic Mechanisms: Regulation of Blood Pressure - THE BULLET POINTS")
**Maintaining Heart rate and rhythm to maintain blood flow**
**Non-contractile tissue - adapted to create a rhythm.**
* Flow of ions (K+,Na+ and Ca2+) through facilitated diffusion through ion channels.
* Fast inflow of Na+ kickstarts depolarisation,
* Slower inflow of Ca2+ maintains depolarisation and contraction, during the middle phases of the action potential, it creates the plateau phase (e.g.ST interval) and trigger muscle contraction;
* Outflow of K+ causes repolarisation and relaxation.
* Rate of flow creates the rhythm.

If the heart does not contract in a rhythmically, coordinated way, blood cannot be circulated in the body, leading to** cardiogenic shock. **The heart's conduction system prevents that from happening.
**Shock would result from an inability to maintain homeostasis**
**Circulatory shock** = when there is **inadequate blood flow to meet the needs of the tissue** , due to some kind of change impacting on blood flow around the body.
Circulatory shock could be caused by anything that makes **blood pressure fall **dramatically, for example:

1. **Hypovolemic shock **= low blood volume as caused by fluid loss (--> low **SV**); bleeding, fluid going into blisters caused by burns, loss of CSF after trauma to the head, dehydration, diarrhea, vomiting,etc.;

2. **Cardiogenic shock **= heart is unable to maintain output (--> low **SV** and low **HR)** e.g. due to damaged conduction system (e.g. by inadequate perfusion to area of it), damaged heart muscle due to ischemia, **heart prevented from contracting efficiently** ;

3. **Obstructive shock** = blood flow to the heart and/or from it is blocked e.g. by blood clots in the vessels to or from the lungs or body or the **heart prevented from filling** as in cardiac tamponade

4. **Anaphylactic shock** = blood vessels dilate and become leaky (permeable) (--> low **SV and ****low **PR) due to allergic reaction with histamine release. Fluid leaves the blood vessels making the blood pressure drop;

5. **Septic shock** = blood vessels dilate and become leaky (--> low **SV and ****low **PR) due to inflammatory response with histamine release. Fluid leaves the blood vessels making the blood pressure drop. Caused by bacteria.** Most common form of shock;**

6. **Neurogenic shock = **when all the blood vessels **dilate (-- > low **PR**) **at once due to loss of sympathetic tone resulting from **damaged sympathetic nerves **e.g. when spinal cord is injured above T6.
**IN THESE CASES DEATH MAY RESULT FROM THE INABILITY OF THE BODY TO MAINTAIN HOMEOSTASIS.**

1\. Blood pressure is determined by cardiac output (how much blood the heart pumps) and peripheral resistance (how narrow or wide the blood vessels are). Blood volume, heart rate, and the elasticity of arteries also affect blood pressure.
2\. High blood pressure (hypertension) is 140/90 mmHg or higher when measured consistently.

3\. High blood pressure can lead to serious long-term health problems, including heart attack, stroke, heart failure, kidney damage, eye damage, and damage to the blood vessels. These complications can reduce a person's quality of life and may be life-threatening if left untreated.

4\. Low blood pressure can cause immediate symptoms such as dizziness, fainting, blurred vision, weakness, confusion, and reduced blood flow to the body's organs. In severe cases, it can lead to shock, which requires urgent medical treatment.

5. Baroreceptors in the carotid arteries and aorta detect the drop in blood pressure and send signals to the brain. The brain increases heart rate, makes the heart pump harder, and narrows blood vessels to raise blood pressure.

6. Baroreceptors detect the increase in blood pressure and signal the brain to slow the heart rate, reduce the force of heart contractions, and widen blood vessels, lowering blood pressure back to normal.

7\. The kidneys release renin, which starts the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). This causes blood vessels to narrow and makes the body retain more salt and water, increasing blood volume and blood pressure.

8\. Quinapril relaxes and widens blood vessels, making it easier for blood to flow. Metoprolol slows the heart rate and reduces how hard the heart pumps. Together they lower blood pressure and reduce the heart's workload, helping prevent damage to the heart, brain, and kidneys.
9\. High blood pressure often has no symptoms but slowly damages blood vessels and organs. Early treatment helps prevent heart attacks, strokes, kidney disease, and other serious complications.
10\. Fatty plaque builds up in the inner lining (tunica intima) of the arteries.
11\. Narrowed blood vessels reduce blood flow and oxygen to tissues. This can cause:
* Legs: Peripheral artery disease causing leg pain when walking

The transport of gases in the blood is a complex chemical process, and it also highly involved in the balance of acids and bases in the body too. This process is integral to human survival. There are many apparatuses and tests that are used in healthcare to monitor blood gases as well! Today we will look at how the gases dissolves and are moved around the body. Of the two main gases exchanged, the transport of CO2 is significantly more complex and has greater overarching impact on the body.

You could have looked at buffers, and how the respiratory system is involved in acid/base balance and homeostasis. For this lecture, I'd like you to refresh your knowledge of the _**respiratory buffer system** _and** **_**chemical buffers** _in general. We are also going to be looking at gases in blood - a fluid. **How the blood carries oxygen and carbon dioxide**

Both Carbon dioxide and Oxygen are carried in the blood by a special iron-containing protein,**hemoglobin.** Around 30-40% of the Carbon dioxide is carried, bound to the amino groups, as **carbaminohemoglobin,** whereas the majority of the oxygen is carried bound to the**heme groups** as **oxyhemoglobin.**

Both Carbon dioxide and Oxygen are carried dissolved in blood plasma. Carbon dioxide is **much more soluble than oxygen in water.** The majority of carbon dioxide is therefore carried either **dissolved** or in the form of **bicarbonate** in the blood. Oxygen is not very soluble in water so only **a small percentage is dissolved** in the blood plasma.
**1\. How does Carbon dioxide bind with hemoglobin?**
* **Carbon-dioxide (CO 2) binds to the amino groups of the hemoglobin to form Carbaminohemoglobin (CO2Hb)**
**2\. Explain the equation that describes how carbon dioxide is transported in the blood.**
**Carbon dioxide + water <\--> Carbonic acid <\---> Bicarbonate ions + Hydrogen ions**
* 70% of carbon dioxide is transported as Bicarbonate ions (HCO3-- = 60-70%),
* Hemoglobin's **amino groups** also bind to carbon dioxide: Carbon dioxide carried as **carbaminohemoglobin** (CO2Hb = 30-40%)
* Carbon dioxide is**highly soluble** in water. when it dissolves in water it forms carbonic acid which dissociates to form bicarbonate and hydrogen ions.
* The reaction can go forwards or backwards (double sided arrows) depending on the relative concentrations of the products/ reagents
* **More CO 2 **would push reaction to the **right **producing more H+ ions (lowering the pH) - more acidic
* L**ess CO 2 **would favour the reaction to the** left** producing less H+ ions (increasing the pH) - more alkaline****

* This reaction forms the basis of the **respiratory buffer system **of the body a **rapid pH-control mechanism** that uses the **lungs to regulate blood pH by controlling carbon dioxide (CO₂) levels**.
**CO₂ = acid ** Change breathing → change CO₂ → change blood pH
**3\. Describe how carbon dioxide is related to pH levels.**

* When CO2 dissolves in water, carbonic acid (H2CO3) is formed. Carbonic acid is a weak acid that dissociates to form H+ ions. The more CO2, the more H+ ions are formed taking the pH down. **Carbon dioxide = acid - the higher the carbon dioxide levels in the blood the more acidic it is. **
**4\. Discuss how forced breathing (hyperventilation) impacts blood pH and why.**

* There should always be low levels of CO2 in the blood to maintain *buffer) the pH within the normal range. With forced breathing, more CO2 is breathed out than is produced by metabolic processes. It causes the reaction CO₂+H₂O↔H₂CO₃↔H⁺+HCO₃⁻) to shift to the **left** with **less hydrogen ions** available to balance (buffer) the blood pH. Without the CO2 present, the blood becomes alkalotic in the process.
* **the amount of carbon dioxide (CO 2) in the blood to drop.**
* **more CO 2 is puffed out than is produced by the body.**
* **the pH of the blood increases (become more alkaline) -a condition known as _respiratory alkalosis_.**
* numbness or tingling in the hands or feet
**5\. Discuss how the respiratory system responds during metabolic acidosis and alkalosis.**
* **Metabolic acidosis **is due to **excess hydrogen** ions in the blood due to conditions such as **diabetes and kidney problems** ,
* There is **too many H+ ions** present in the blood.
* The respiratory system tries to compensate for this overabundance of H+ ions by **increasing breathing rate (Kussmaul respiration)** to get rid of CO2 and in doing so, increasing the pH.
* **Metabolic alkalosis** is due to a **shortage of hydrogen ions **in the blood due to conditions such as **vomiting** and i**ntake of antacids** ,
* There are too few H+ ions present in the blood.
* The respiratory system tries to compensate for this shortage of H+ ions by **decreasing breathing rate** to **retain** more CO2 and in doing so, decreasing the pH.
**1\. Discuss how hemoglobin carries oxygen and how it behaves differently under different conditions (the Bohr effect). **

_"The basic rhythm of the respiratory cycle of inspiration and expiration seems to be generated by the **medullary rhythmicity area.** This area of the medulla consists of two regions of interconnected control centres: the dorsal respiratory group (DRG) and the ventral respiratory group (VRG).** The VRG seems to be the basic rhythm generator** in animal models and thus may also serve this function in human beings. Normal, quiet breathing rhythm is generated by alternating patterns of stimulation and inhibition of motor neurons that signal the muscles of the diaphragm. The DRG integrates information from chemoreceptors for P co 2 and signals the **VRG** to alter the breathing rhythm to restore homeostasis._

_A current hypothesis suggests that the basic breathing rhythm can be altered by different inputs to the medullary rhythmicity area. For example, input from a possible **apneustic centre** in the pons may regulate the length and depth of inspiration. Damage to the nerves from the apneustic centre is thought to produce breathing characterized by abnormally long, deep inspirations, which is sometimes called “apneustic breathing”._

_The **pontine respiratory group** (PRG; formerly called the _pneumotaxic centre_ ), also in the pons, may regulate both the apneustic centre and the medullary rhythmicity area. Thus a network of interconnected centres in the brainstem regulates the rhythm of breathing.)"_

The alternate movement of air into and out of the lungs that we call breathing can occur in distinctive patterns that can be recognized and designated by name (see [figure](https://www-clinicalkey-com.ezproxy.manukau.ac.nz/student/nursing/content/book/3-s2.0-B978070207860600050X#f5025) ).
Examples of breathing patterns and spirograms.

* **Eupnoea** = term used to describe **normal quiet** breathing. During eupnoea, the need for oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange is being met, and the individual is not usually conscious of the breathing pattern. Ventilation occurs spontaneously at the rate of **12 to 17** breaths per minute.

* **Hyperpnoea =** increased breathing that is regulated to **meet an increased demand** by the body for oxygen--> increased pulmonary ventilation. If caused by exercise because of increased oxygen need: increase in tidal volume alone or by an increase in both tidal volume and breathing frequency.

* **Hyperventilation =** increase in pulmonary ventilation in **excess of the need for oxygen**. May be due to **conscious** voluntary effort preceding exertion or from **psychogenic** factors (hysterical hyperventilation). Result in reduced levels of CO2. in the blood--> **respiratory alkalosis** (seen in panic attacks).
* **Hypoventilation** = decrease in pulmonary ventilation that results in elevated blood levels of CO2 \--> **respiratory acidosis** (seen in COPD).

* **Dyspnoea** = laboured or difficult breathing and is often associated with hypoventilation. A person suffering from dyspnoea is aware, or conscious, of the breathing pattern and is generally uncomfortable and in distress.
* **Orthopnoea** =dyspnoea _while lying down_. It is relieved by sitting or standing up. Common in patients with heart disease.

* **Kussmaul breathing (compensatory hyperventilation) =** abnormal, deep, rapid, and labored breathing pattern. An automatic, involuntary response to severe **metabolic** **acidosis.** The body attempts to **compensate** by "blowing off" excess CO**2** to raise blood pH.
* **Compensatory hypoventilation =** abnormal, shallow, slow, breathing pattern seen in **metabolic alkalosis**. An effort to retain CO2.
Several terms are used to describe **breathing cessation**.
* **Apnoea** =temporary cessation of breathing at the end of a normal expiration. It may occur during sleep or when swallowing.
* **Apneusis** = cessation of breathing in the inspiratory position. Failure to resume breathing after a period of apnoea, or apneusis, is called **respiratory arrest.**

* **Cheyne–Stokes respiration** = periodic type of abnormal breathing often seen in **terminally ill** or **brain-damaged** patients. It is characterized by cycles of gradually increasing tidal volume for several breaths followed by several breaths with gradually decreasing tidal volume. These cycles repeat in a type of crescendo-decrescendo pattern.

1. What are the pleural membranes, and what is their function?
The pleural membranes are two thin membranes that surround the lungs: the visceral pleural and the parietal pleural. Their function is to reduce friction and help keep the lungs expanded.
2\. What is the function of the facial cavities (the oral and nasal cavities)?
The nasal and oral cavities provide a pathway for air to enter the respiratory system. The nasal cavity also warms, humidifies and filters inspired air.
3\. Can you explain why the epiglottis is important?
The epiglottis closes over the entrance to the larynx during swallowing, preventing food and fluid from entering the trachea and lungs.
4\. Can you explain how the body stops particles from entering the lungs?

Mucus and cilia: Nasal hairs – act as a filter and trap particles and eventually get stuck in mucus; Carina – right at the bottom of the trachea – stimulates the cough reflex; Epiglottis – prevents large objects form entering the trachea – not effective against small particles.
5\. What is the pathway that air takes as it moves into the lungs?

Conducting zone: Nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → terminal bronchioles. Respiratory zone: Respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveoli. Nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
6\. How would you explain the alveoli to a non-health person?
Alveoli are tiny air sacs in the lungs where oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide moves out of the blood.
7\. What are type 1 and type 2 cells of the alveoli? _Type 1 is for gaseous exchange and type 2 is for producing surfactant_

Type II alveolar cells secrete a chemical substance called surfactant; Type I alveolar cells form part of the respiratory membrane; Surfactant helps to reduce surface tension in the lungs; Macrophages protect the alveoli from bacterial invasion
8\. Explain what the respiratory membrane is and how it is relevant.

The respiratory membrane is a very thin barrier between the alveoli and pulmonary capillaries. It consists mainly of the alveolar epithelium, basement membrane and capillary endothelium. It is important because oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across it during gas exchange. Its thin structure allows rapid and efficient gas exchange.

Lymph is derived from the**fluid that has leaked from the arteriolar end** of the capillaries in the CVS that forms the **tissue fluid** (or interstitial fluid). Some of this fluid is collected by the venous end of the capillary but if it doesn't, this fluid enters the lymphatic system through lymphatic capillaries;

**Patton: FIGURE 31-5: Circulation plan of lymphatic fluid.**
_This diagram outlines the general scheme for lymphatic circulation._
_1\. Fluids from the systemic and pulmonary capillaries leave the bloodstream and enter the interstitial space, thus becoming part of the interstitial fluid (IF)._
_2\. The IF also exchanges materials with the surrounding tissues._
_3\. Often, because less fluid is returned to the blood capillary than had left it,**IF pressure increases—causing IF to flow into the lymphatic capillary.**_
_4\. The fluid is then called lymph (lymphatic fluid) and is carried through one or more lymph nodes and finally to large lymphatic ducts. _
_5\. About 3 litres of fluid returns to the systemic blood plasma per day as lymph that enters a subclavian vein._
_6\. Thus fluid circulates through blood vessels, tissues, and lymphatic vessels in a sort of “open circulation”._
**Factors that aid in unidirectional flow of lymph back to systemic circulation ( lymphokinesis):**
1\. Large number of **unidirectional** **valves** that permit fluid flow only in the central direction.

2\. **Breathing movements** (inspiration establishes a pressure gradient in the thoracic duct causing lymph to flow upward through it. The flow rate of lymph into the venous circulation is proportional to the depth of inspiration (Patton, 2019).

3\. **Skeletal muscle contractions** "milk” the lymphatic vessels and push the lymph forward ( Patton [Figure 31-7](https://www-clinicalkey-com.ezproxy.manukau.ac.nz/student/nursing/content/book/3-s2.0-B9780702078606000444#f0070) ).

Mary developed **lymphoedema** because some axillary lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels were removed or damaged during surgery.

Normally, capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes some fluid out of the blood capillaries into the interstitial space. Most of this fluid returns to the blood, while the remaining excess fluid and proteins are collected by lymphatic vessels.
Major functions of the lymphatic system
1. Fluid balance: Collect excess interstitial fluid from tissue spaces, return it back to the blood circulation, preventing tissue oedema.
2. Immune defence: Lymph nodes filter lymph; immune cells (lymphocytes, macrophages) remove bacteria, foreign particles and abnormal cells, mount immune responses.
3. Fat absorption: Lacteals in intestinal villi absorb dietary lipids (chyle) and transport them into blood circulation.
2\. Role of axillary lymph nodes in cancer spread
Axillary lymph nodes drain lymph fluid from the breast and upper‑limb tissues.
\- Cancer cells from a breast tumour can enter local lymphatic vessels and travel within lymph fluid to axillary lymph nodes.
\- Lymph nodes try to trap malignant cells. If cancer cells survive and multiply inside the node, the lymph node becomes metastatic.
\- Tumour cells may then spread further through the lymphatic system to other nodes or enter bloodstream for distant metastasis.
Axillary node status is a key indicator for breast‑cancer staging
Mastectomy often removes or damages axillary lymph nodes and local lymphatic vessels.
\- Normally, excess fluid continuously filters out of capillaries into interstitial (tissue) spaces. The lymphatic system drains this interstitial fluid away.
\- After surgery, the lymphatic drainage pathways of the right arm are destroyed / blocked.
\- Interstitial fluid cannot be adequately removed from arm tissue spaces. Fluid accumulates within interstitial compartments → swelling (lymphoedema).
\- Fluid keeps moving out of blood capillaries into tissue space, while outflow via lymphatics is impaired, so fluid builds‑up persistently.

2. What is the structure of lymph nodes, and what is found in them?
* Small, bean-shaped organs with a capsule.
* Contain B cells, T cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and lymph fluid that filters germs.
3. Which cells find antigens in the body?
* Dendritic cells and macrophages detect and capture antigens.
4. Which cells stimulate a full immune response, and how?
* Dendritic cells present the antigen to helper T cells, which activate B cells to make antibodies and cytotoxic T cells to destroy infected cells.
* Vaccines expose the body to a safe form of an antigen, allowing the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells without causing the disease.
6. How does the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine work differently?
* It contains mRNA, which tells body cells to make a harmless spike protein. The immune system recognizes the protein and builds immunity. It does not contain the virus or change your DNA.
7. What is the difference between vaccination and immunisation?
* Vaccination: The act of receiving a vaccine.
* Immunisation: The protection that develops after the immune system responds to the vaccine (or an infection).
1\. Where in the body are B- and T- lymphocytes made and stored?

B- and T-lymphocytes both originate from stem cells in the bone marrow. B-cells mature in the bone marrow, while T-cells mature in the thymus. After maturation, they circulate and are stored mainly in lymph nodes, the spleen, and other lymphoid tissues.
2\. What is the structure of lymph nodes, and what is found in lymph nodes?

A lymph node has a capsule, cortex, paracortex, and medulla. Afferent vessels bring lymph in, and efferent it out. The cortex mainly has B cells, the paracortex mainly has T cells, and the medulla contains plasma cells and macrophages.
3. Which cells in the body will find antigens in the body?
Dendritic cells, macrophages, and B-lymphocytes are antigen-presenting cells. Dendritic cells are the most important for activating T cells. Dendritic cells start the adaptive immune response.
4. Which cells will stimulate a full-on immune response against an antigen, and how?
A full on immune response is mainly initiated by dendritic cells and activated helper T cells. Helper T cells release cytokines and activate B cells, cytotoxic T cells, and macrophages.
A vaccine gives the immune system a safe antigen or instruction for making one. The body produces antibodies and memory B and T cells. Later exposure causes a faster and stronger response.
6. The Covid-19 vaccine is an RNA vaccine. How does this vaccine work differently from others?

Covid-19: mRNA gives cells temporary instructions to make a harmless piece of spike protein. The immune system recognizes it and forms antibodies and memory cells. The mRNA is then broken down. It doesn't enter the nucleus or change DNA.
7\. What is the difference between vaccination and immunisation?
Vaccination is receiving or giving a vaccine. Immunisation is the process of developing protection or immuning.
1\. Where are B and T lymphocytes made and stored?
B cells are made and mature in the bone marrow. They are stored in the lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils, and other lymphatic tissues.
T cells are also made in the bone marrow, but they mature in the thymus gland. After maturing, they are stored in the lymph nodes, spleen, and other lymphatic tissues.
2\. What is the structure of lymph nodes, and what is found in them?
Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped organs connected by lymph vessels. They help filter germs from the lymph fluid.
They contain B cells, T cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and plasma cells. These cells work together to fight infection.
3\. Which cells find antigens in the body?
The main cells that find antigens are dendritic cells and macrophages. B cells can also recognise some antigens.
These cells look for germs and other foreign substances in the body.
4\. Which cells start a full immune response, and how?
Dendritic cells start the immune response. They capture the antigen and carry it to the lymph nodes.
There, they show the antigen to helper T cells. The helper T cells activate B cells to make antibodies and killer T cells to destroy infected cells.
A vaccine contains a safe form of an antigen, not the real disease.
The immune system learns to recognise the antigen and makes antibodies and memory cells. If the real germ enters the body later, it can fight it quickly.
6\. How does the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine work?
The COVID-19 mRNA vaccine does not contain the virus. It contains mRNA, which tells your cells to make a harmless spike protein.
Your immune system recognises the spike protein as foreign and makes antibodies and memory cells. The mRNA is then broken down and does not change your DNA.
7\. What is the difference between vaccination and immunisation?
Vaccination is the act of receiving a vaccine.
Immunisation is the protection your body develops after the vaccine. This happens when your immune system creates antibodies and memory cells.
The Lymphatic system's main function is maintain fluid balance - returning the fluid that leaked out of the capillary vessels back to the blood circulation.

Fluid filters faster out of the arterial sides of the capillary beds than it flows back due to high hydrostatic pressure and low oncotic pressure. On the venous side the situation is reversed so that more fluid returns to the blood vessels because high oncotic pressure favours reabsorption over filtration.

However, not all fluid filters back to the blood system. A significant amount remains in the interstitial spaces between the cells. This is where the lymphatic system comes in: to return this remaining fluid.
The blind ending lymphatic **capillaries** have**** one way mini valves that allows **interstitial fluid** to enter but not leave it.
Once in the lymph capillaries, the fluid is called **lymph**.
The sequence from the left toe to the blood stream can be described as:
* Blind ending lymph capillaries with mini valves-->
* (afferent lymph vessels-->lymph node--> efferent lymph vessels) (n) -->
**Lymphedema** occurs when a blockage or trauma to the lymph nodes or vessels interrupt lymph reabsorption and flow.
**Edema** (swelling) may also occur in the following conditions:

1\. **INCREASED HYDROSTATIC PRESSURE: Hypertension** increases hydrostatic pressure on the arterial side of the capillary bed so that **increased filtration** makes much more fluid leave the capillary beds than can be reabsorbed on the venous side.

2\. **LEAKY BLOODVESSELS** : **Anaphylaxis and** **inflammation** lead to release of chemicals such as histamine which make the blood vessels more permeable (leaky) than usual. Fluid leaks out into the tissues in higher volumes than can be reabsorbed.

3\. **INADEQUATE ONCOTIC PRESSURE** : **A low protein diet** (such as in kwashiorkor) or **loss of protein** (e.g. in damaged kidney glomeruli) may make the protein content of the blood too low to muster enough oncotic pressure to reabsorb the fluid.

Edema has a negative impact on cells in the affected areas since it **increases the diffusion distance** between the blood (source of O2 and nutrients) and the particular cells.Some cells may end up using anaerobic respiration or starving.
It further becomes a challenge for these cells to get rid of CO2 and other waste products.

1. **What determines blood pressure? You’ll need to think about our physiology as well as those factors that can change our blood pressure.**
**HM: Can be summed up by equation: BP = SV x HR x PR**
* **Cardiac Output (CO)-** amount of blood your heart pumps **per minute = SV x HR**
* **Peripheral resistance-** How narrow/ wide your blood vessels are. pushback by arteries
* **Blood Volume** \- more blood= higher pressure. Dehydration = lower blood pressure.**= Stroke volume (SV)**
* Hormones and kidneys- regulation of sodium and water balance, all effecting bp. **because they affect SV by affecting blood volume**
* Blood pressure is measured in two parts:
* 1\. the **systolic pressure** (when the heart contracts) and
* 2\. the**diastolic pressure** (when the heart relaxes). these two parts can be further broken down into atrial systolic, atrial diastole, ventricular systole, and ventricular diastole.
* However, there are numerous factors that influence changes in blood pressure such as

### Blood pressure is determined by several factors related to both the heart and blood vessels. It is the force that blood exerts on the walls of arteries as it is pumped by the heart. Blood pressure is influenced by:
1. **Cardiac Output** : The amount of blood the heart pumps per minute. The higher the cardiac output, the higher the blood pressure.

2. **Peripheral Resistance** : The resistance that blood encounters as it flows through blood vessels, mainly in the arteries. If arteries constrict (narrow), resistance increases, and so does blood pressure.
3. **Blood Volume** : The total amount of blood in the circulatory system. More blood increases pressure.
4. **Blood Viscosity** : Thicker blood (higher viscosity) increases resistance and, consequently, blood pressure.
5. **Elasticity of the Arteries** : Healthy, flexible arteries allow for more efficient blood flow. If the arteries become stiff (e.g., due to arteriosclerosis), blood pressure can rise.
**2\. High blood pressure is defined as?**

* High blood pressure in medical terminology is referred to as **hypertension,** directly translating to **excessive (hyper-) pressure (-tension).** High blood pressure means the **pressure being exerted on the walls of arteries** and blood vessels is**high/higher than usual. **
**3\. High blood pressure has several chronic, downstream consequences. What are they? Thinking about the implications for long-term health and wellness, as well as why we care as nurses!**
**Heart problems, Stroke, Eye damage, damage to the kidneys, risk of type 2 diabetes. **

Hypertension is often called the "silent killer" because it can cause significant long-term damage before symptoms appear. As nurses, we care about these consequences because they affect patient outcomes, increase the risk of hospitalization, and require long-term management.
1. **Cardiovascular Disease (CVD)** – Chronic hypertension strains the heart, leading to:
* **Left Ventricular Hypertrophy** → The heart muscle thickens, reducing its efficiency and increasing the risk of heart failure.
* **Heart Failure** → The heart becomes too weak to pump blood effectively.
* **Coronary Artery Disease** → Increased pressure damages arteries, increasing the risk of heart attacks.
2. **Stroke (Ischemic & Hemorrhagic)** – Damaged blood vessels in the brain can rupture or become blocked, leading to stroke and long-term neurological impairment.
**4\. Low blood pressure has several acute consequences. These are?**
* **Dizziness, fainting, shock, fatigue, and kidney injury. If untreated, it can cause organ damage and be life-threatening.**
1. **Dizziness and Lightheadedness** – Reduced blood flow to the brain can cause a feeling of unsteadiness.
2. **Fainting (Syncope)** – A sudden drop in blood pressure may lead to temporary loss of consciousness.

3. **Shock (Severe Hypotension)** – Critically low blood pressure can deprive organs of oxygen and lead to life-threatening conditions such as **septic shock, cardiogenic shock, or anaphylactic shock**.
4. **Blurred Vision** – Insufficient blood flow to the eyes can cause visual disturbances.
5. **Confusion or Difficulty Concentrating** – The brain may not receive enough oxygen, leading to mental fog or confusion.
6. **Cold, Clammy, or Pale Skin** – Poor circulation can cause the skin to appear pale and feel cool or sweaty.
7. **Rapid, Shallow Breathing** – The body may compensate for low blood pressure by increasing respiration.
8. **Weak or Rapid Pulse** – The heart may beat faster to try to stabilize circulation.

_You have nervous system processes that help to keep your blood pressure steady at rest and help to increase or decrease it back to normal for exercise or after exercise, based on feedback from your body. **5\. How does the nervous system detect and return blood pressure to normal when it is lower than normal (e.g. you’ve just stood up quickly and BP to your brain drops; thnx gravity – as for Jack’s postural hypotension)**

* then medulla oblongata activates the **parasympathetic nervous system(PNS)** via vagus nerve,
* **vasomotor centre activates the parasympathetic nervous system** -**vasodilation** occurs,

**8\. What are Jack’s medications trying to do? Explain in plain, easy-to-understand language! Relate it back to the processes you described in questions 6 and 7!**
* Metoprol**ol** is a cardio selective **beta-blocker,** which suppresses the heart and lowers the heart rate. This leads to decreased heart rate, cardiac contractility, and cardiac output.

* Quin**april i** s an angiotensin converting enzyme **(ACE) inhibitor.** Angiotensin-converting enzyme is responsible for converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II that stimulates the release of aldosterone, ADH, increases thirst and vasoconstriction that decreases blood pressure. So, by taking this medication Angiotensin II does not get released. So, this medication keeps the arterial blood pressure in the normal range.
**9\. Why are medications for high blood pressure started when there are no symptoms of damage?**
* High blood pressure or chronic blood pressure is considered a **silent killer** and

* Still, slowly it can strain the heart and damages the arteries.

_Atherosclerosis is the process by which blood vessels can become narrowed because a fatty plaque builds up in the blood vessel. This narrowing can prevent blood from flowing though the vessel, and even end up blocking the vessel. If this happens in the coronary vessels, this can cause angina, chest pain, or worse!_
**10\. Where does the fatty deposit build-up?**

The fatty deposits, also known as plaques, build up in the arterial walls. This process is called atherosclerosis and primarily occurs in medium and large arteries, such as the coronary arteries, carotid arteries, and peripheral arteries.
* **_These fatty deposits build up in the tunica intima of the medium and large arteries._**

**11\. What does narrowing a blood vessel and preventing/restriction blood flow cause? What are some examples of these around the body?**
* Narrowing a blood vessel reduces the amount of oxygenated blood that can reach the tissues,
* If the blockage becomes severe, it can completely cut off blood supply, leading to tissue damage or death.
Examples of Atherosclerosis in Different Areas of the Body:
* Causes angina (chest pain) can lead to a heart attack (myocardial infarction) if completely blocked
* Reduces blood flow to the brain
* Increases the risk of stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA, mini-stroke)
3. Peripheral Arteries (Legs, Arms) → Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD)

Atherosclerosis is a progressive disease, meaning it gets worse over time, and can be life-threatening if not managed properly with lifestyle changes, medications, or medical interventions like angioplasty or bypass surgery.

_Over the last 2 years, the importance of vaccinations have been shown. In 2019 we saw a measles pandemic, and a few months later, the COVID-19 pandemic began. You might need to in the future, provide education about what vaccination is, what immunisation is, how it works, and why it is important._

_Vaccination works by stimulating the immune system (to go through a practice run) with an antigen, but not the actual pathogen. It’s kind of like when someone shares a screenshot of someone on FB that is scamming folks on marketplace – they show your brain a picture of what to look out for, so if you see this person selling on market place, you know to avoid or shut down! This practice run works on the acquired immune system, the T and B lymphocytes._
1\. Where in the body are B and T lymphocytes made and stored? Be specific!
2\. What is the structure of a lymph nodes, and what is found in lymph nodes?
* The lymph node is enclosed by a fibrous outer layer called the capsule. This provides structural support and protection for the node.

* The outer region of the lymph node is called the cortex. The cortex contains clusters of immune cells called B lymphocytes and follicles (also called lymphoid follicles), where B-cells are activated in response to antigens.

* Beneath the cortex is the paracortex, which contains T lymphocytes (T-cells). This area is also where the immune cells are activated by antigens and where interactions between B-cells and T-cells occur.

* The medulla is the inner portion of the lymph node. It contains medullary cords, which are made up of lymphocytes (mainly B-cells), macrophages, and plasma cells. This is where the final steps of immune responses take place, including the production of antibodies.

* The lymph node contains sinuses, which are channels that allow lymph to flow through the node. These sinuses help filter out pathogens, debris, and other foreign particles as the lymph flows through the node.

* Lymph enters the node through afferent lymphatic vessels and exits through efferent lymphatic vessels. The afferent vessels bring lymph from the tissues, while the efferent vessels drain filtered lymph away from the node.
* B lymphocytes (B-cells): These are found primarily in the cortex and are responsible for producing antibodies in response to pathogens.
* T lymphocytes (T-cells): Found mainly in the paracortex, T-cells help in recognizing and killing infected cells or coordinating the immune response.
* Macrophages: Found throughout the lymph node, these cells help engulf and digest pathogens and debris.
* Plasma cells: These are activated B-cells that have differentiated to secrete antibodies.

* The fluid that circulates through the lymphatic system, carrying white blood cells, proteins, waste products, and sometimes pathogens or foreign particles, which the immune cells within the lymph node work to filter and destroy.
3\. Which cells in the body will find antigens in the body?
* **Dendritic cells** and **macrophages** capture and present antigens.
* **T-cells** identify infected cells and help coordinate the immune response.
* **Natural Killer T-cells** destroy abnormal cells directly.
4\. Which cells will stimulate a full on immune response against an antigen, and how?
* **Helper T Cells (CD4+ T cells)** : **Master regulators** —they initiate and coordinate the entire immune response.
* **Cytotoxic T Cells (CD8+ T cells)** : **Kill infected cells** after activation by Helper T cells.
* **B Cells** : **Produce antibodies** to target and neutralise antigens after stimulation from Helper T cells.
* **Macrophages and Dendritic Cells** : **Present antigens** to activate Helper T cells and enhance inflammation.
5\. How does vaccination work? How does the COVID-19 vaccine work?

Vaccination **trains the immune system** to recognise and fight pathogens (like viruses or bacteria) **without causing the disease**. It does this by introducing a harmless form of the pathogen (or a part of it) to stimulate an immune response. Here’s a breakdown of the process:
* The vaccine contains a **weakened** , **inactivated** , or **synthetic** version of a pathogen (e.g., a virus or bacteria) or specific parts of it (e.g., proteins or genetic material).
* **Antigen-presenting cells (APCs)** (like **dendritic cells**) detect the vaccine’s antigen and present it to **Helper T cells**.
* Activate **Cytotoxic T cells** to destroy infected cells if the real virus appears.
* After the immune system responds to the vaccine, **memory B cells** and **memory T cells** remain in the body.
* These memory cells provide **long-term protection** by responding **faster and stronger** if the person is exposed to the actual pathogen later.
* If the vaccinated person encounters the real virus or bacteria, their immune system can **recognise and destroy it quickly** , preventing severe illness.

There are several types of COVID-19 vaccines, but the most widely used (such as **mRNA vaccines** and **viral vector vaccines**) work by teaching the body to produce a harmless part of the virus—the **spike protein** —which triggers an immune response. Here’s how each type functions:
* The vaccine contains **messenger RNA (mRNA)** —a genetic blueprint for the **SARS-CoV-2 spike protein**.
* Once injected, the mRNA enters muscle cells but does **not** interact with human DNA.
* The cells use the mRNA to **produce the spike protein** , which is displayed on their surface.
* The immune system identifies the spike protein as **foreign**.
* **Helper T cells** trigger B cells to produce **antibodies** against the spike protein.
* **Cytotoxic T cells** are activated to destroy infected cells if the virus enters the body.
* After the mRNA is broken down (in a few hours or days), the immune system retains **memory cells** that can quickly respond if the real virus is encountered.
* These vaccines use a **harmless virus** (like an adenovirus) to deliver genetic instructions for the **SARS-CoV-2 spike protein**.
* The body’s cells produce the spike protein, triggering the immune system to recognise it.
* Similar to mRNA vaccines, **antibodies** and **memory T cells** form to protect against future infections.
6\. What is the difference between vaccination and immunisation?
* **Definition** : The **act of administering a vaccine** (by injection, oral drops, or nasal spray) to stimulate the body’s immune system against a specific disease.
* **Purpose** : To **expose the immune system to a safe version** of a pathogen (or part of it) without causing illness.
* **Example** : Receiving the COVID-19 vaccine through an injection is **vaccination**.
* **Definition** : The **process by which a person becomes protected** from an infectious disease after vaccination. This includes developing **antibodies** and **immune memory**.
* **Purpose** : To provide **long-term protection** against future infections by priming the immune system.
* **Example** : If your body produces **antibodies** and **memory cells** after receiving a vaccine, you have achieved **immunisation**.

The spinal cord and spinal nerves represent one of the transition points from CNS to PNS. The spinal cord is comprised for grey and white matter, and I like to imagine it as looking like a butterfly within an overdrawn set of lips! It's certainly a stretch but can you see it?

The butterfly is the grey matter - this is where the cell bodies of neurons are, and you can see the grey matter is found in the middle, the opposite to the brain! The lips are the white matter tracts, the axons of those neurons connecting the brain to the body! On the image below it shows the different parts of the white matter, the nerve tracts, with the blue part carrying information TO the brain, and the red parts carrying information FROM the brain. You can see it's very distinctly organised! It is not important to remember these tracts, I just wanted you to see how specific each part of the nervous system is!

The Autonomic nervous system; which covers the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system includes SOME but not ALL of the peripheral nerves. The image below shows the origins of the SNS and PSNS The PSNS has a craniosacral origin - from 4 cranial nerves (3, 7, 9 and 10) and 3 sacral spinal nerves (S2-S4). The SNS has what we call a thoracolumbar origin - from T1-L2, the thoracic and lumbar nerves, and forms a chain of sympathetic ganglia (a ganglion/ganglia is just a group of neurons!) The reflex arc allows the peripheral nervous system to stimulate predictable action in the body. What I mean by this that a reflex is a consistent response to a particular stimulus. Since the response is consistent, the same every time, you can hardwire it into the spinal cord, so you don't need the brain involved in that decision. We do this using interneurons. Spinal nerves, come from your spinal cord, and take information to and from your CNS (spinal cord) to the body. The spinal nerves are related to the different vertebrae of the spine, though in humans, our vertebral spine has some bones that have become fused, so there is not a one to one ratio.

The spinal nerves are where the nerves leave the spinal cord, and there is a special organisation and structure at this point, which we will explore more after the break when we look at reflexes, but the spinal nerves don't have special names, they are just organised into groups and numbered. Gustation (our sense of taste) and Olfaction (our sense of smell) are caleld chemical senses, as they involve receptors on sensory neurons binding to chemical compounds and sending signals to our brains for processing. These are one of the ways that we get information about our world, and chemical senses are thought to be the oldest kind of sense in the world. Even bacteria have the ability to sense the chemicals in the environment around them. For humans, we tend to think of these are less important senses, as we rely heavily on vision and hearing, but, these senses are still important and amazing processes!

The Olfactory Bulb are two structures of the brain that lay on the underside of the brain, and neurons from the olfactory bulbs poke down, through the skull into the roof of the nasal cavity, where volatile compounds (those things that we smell) come into contact with the receptors on the neurons!

An interesting thing about the olfactory bulb is that the neurons are able to be replaced, and are part of something called the rostral migratory stream, where stem cells from the subventricular zone (near the ventricles of the brain) grow and divide to create cells that will travel to the olfactory bulb to replace old cells. And this was actually discovered by a research group here in NZ! <https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0079612309175039> is a link to the article about it!

This TEXTBOOK READING [Chapter 24, Sense of Smell, Patton and Thibbodeau](https://www.clinicalkey.com/student/nursing/content/book/3-s2.0-B9780702078606000365#hl0001233) shows the organisation of the neurons in the olfactory bulb. The human olfactory system is a lot more sensitive than you'd think, and there is a wide variation in individuals, in both their sensitivity (how low a concentration they can detect) and their ability to smell different compounds!

22\. Complete the genetics glossary below. They are in no particular order, and some related words are close together in the list, or further apart!

Mitosis | The process of cell division that results in _____________ identical (but not necessarily functionally identical) daughter cells. These daughter cells will have _______________chromosomes (______________pairs), and they will be diploid (having ___________ set of chromosomes, 1 maternal and 1 paternal).

Meiosis | The process of cell division that results in ______________ genetically varied daughter cells that function as gametes (egg cells and sperm cells). Only occurs in your _________________, and each daughter cell will have 23 chromosomes (1 set) and haploid (1 set chromosomes).

Variation | The fact that humans have ____________________, and their complement of genes (that make up their genome) can be very different to others. This variation is important for health and wellbeing. When populations have low genetic variation, they can be more susceptible to disease and genetic issues.
Gene | A sequence of ___________ that codes for a protein. That protein will carry out a function in the body!
DNA | The genetic material that contains all the instructions for the body's function.
Chromatin | DNA isn't found by itself, in the nucleus, it is package up and wound around special proteins. These proteins and DNA together are called chromatin.
Chromosome | A chromosome is a ______________that is inherited together - certain genes are found on certain chromosomes! Humans have 46 chromosomes, 23 from mum and 23 from dad.
Autosome | A chromosome that is not a _______chromosome and so does not contribute to genetic sex. Autosomes in humans are numbered 1-22

Sex Chromosome | A chromosome that contributes to genetic sex. In humans these are the ___________ chromosomes, and most people have 2, a pair of sex chromosomes, with an X from mum, and either an X or Y from dad (but there are other genetic sex combos as well!).
Haploid | A cell with only ________ of each chromosome. Our gametes (eggs and sperm) are haploid and have 23 chromosomes
Diploid | A cell with __________ of each chromosome. Our body cells are diploid and have 23 pairs of chromosomes, for a total of 46 chromosomes.

Aneuploidy | When a person has an abnormal ________of chromsomes - usually an extra, or missing 1. There are a few different aneuploidies, but common ones are Down Syndrome (or Trisomy 21 when a person inherits an extra chromosome 21), Turners syndrome (when a person have only 1 sex chromosome and so their genetic sex is XO), or Klinefelters syndrome (when a person has 2 X chromosomes and 1 Y chromsome).

Polyploidy | Polyploid is when something has ______________ SETS of chromosomes, and can be triploid (3 copies of each chromosome), tetraploid (4) and so on. This is very rare in human reproduction, but can occur in liver and placenta cells!

Disjunction and Non-Disjunction | Disjunction is when chromosomes divide during meiosis. In meiosis 2, sister chromatids that make up a chromosome are split into 2 new chromosomes, and end up in different gametes. When this doesn't happen properly, it is called non-disjunction, and gametes end up with extra chromosomes or missing chromosomes (ie 1 gametes gets 2 chromosomes, and the other gamete made in the same division gets none!)

Cell division | The process by which a cell splits into two new cells. The parent cells must be large enough and have duplicates of their DNA and organelles so the two new cells have their own machinery.
Pro, Meta, Ana, Telophases | The different stages of mitosis (and meiosis)
Gamete | In humans, this is a haploid _____________ cell that will be used for sexual reproduction - a male and female gamete join to create a zygote!

Dominant | A version of a gene that is always expressed in a _____________________ (the traits/things that we see in our body). The dominant allele is like your loud friend, if they are there, you're always going to hear them!

Recessive | A version of a gene that you only see in the phenotype or trait of a person if there is none of the dominant version in other words when there are ___________ recessive ones. The reccessive allele is like that friend you have that everyone think is shy and quiet, but as soon as everyone leaves, they turn into the nutjob you know and love :)

Codominant | When you have codominance, you have 2 dominant alleles. So that is like having two loud friends, and they just talk over each other all the time! There are traits we have where 2 version can be expressed at the same time. The best example is human blood groups. A and B alleles are both _______________, which is why you have A blood, B blood AND AB blood which has both. O blood group is the __________________!

Incomplete Dominance | Incomplete dominance is when you have two alleles, and neither one is really properly dominant. A good example is flowers, where you have a red version, and a white version of the gene for colour, but when you have BOTH versions you end up with ____________! SO not quite red, not quite white. You dont see this much in humans, Sickle Cell disease is really the only example. In Sickle cell disease, if you have both a normal gene and a disease gene, half your RBCS are sickle shaped and half are normal. This mix means a person won't have the symptoms of sickle cell disease (which is bad), but! they are resistant to malaria!
Monogenic | When ___________gene creates a trait. Some examples of monogenic traits are: Attached or unattached ear lobes, middle digit hair, where there distinct options, or groups of traits.

Polygenic | When _______________ genes create a trait. Some examples of polygenetic traits are things that have a spectrum, like height, body size, hair colour, body shape, eye colour, voice, skin colour \- there isn't necessarily specific groups, e.g. blonde vs brown is subjective.

Allele | Are what we call the different versions of genes, and they can be recessive or dominant! For example, a gene could have a normal and diseased version - they would each be alleles. We commonly use eye colour alleles to think about this too.
Genotype | These are the genes you got. Your genetic makeup. For example, a person might have an A allele and an O allele for their blood type.
Phenotype | This is the trait you have - what is expressed. The person above, with AO alleles for blood type would have Type A Blood.
Trait | The trait is something that you are inheriting from your parents, and it based on your genes
Mutation | Mutation is caused when something causes your DNA to __________. Things like UV rays can cause mutations in your DNA sequence.
Zygote | When an ________ and ___________join together, they form a zygote, the beginning of a new organism.
Homozygote | When you have two alleles that are the _________
Heterozygote | When you have two alleles that are ______________
Punnet Square (Aka Monohybrid Cross) | A methods to figure out what genotypes are possible in children of two parents
Pedigree Chart | A family tree of the genes of different people. We can use these to figure out the genotypes of different people in a family based on the phenotypes of different people.
Karyotype | A diploid complement of homologous chromosomes - all the chromosomes you have in each cell! ![](https://cdn.arstechnica.net/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/nci-vol-2721-300.jpg)

Mitochondrial DNA | Your mitochondria have their own DNA! People only inherit their mitochondrial DNA from their mum, so mitochondrial DNA diseases only pass from mother to child. There is an article here [Article: Sperm Mitophagy and Mitochondrial DNALinks to an external site.](https://www.publish.csiro.au/RD/RD17364) about how any sperm mitochondria is destroyed so only egg mitochondria are found in the new zygote!
Trisomy | When you have 3 copies of a chromosome when you should only have two. The most common trisomy is Trisomy 21, or Down's Syndrome

Chorionic Villus Sampling | A genetic testing protocol, where a part of the placenta (called the chorionic villus) is extracted from the uterus for genetic testing. The chorionic villus has the same DNA as the fetus (as it is made from cells that come from the zygote).
Amniocentesis | A genetic testing protocol where some of the amniotic fluid is removed from the uterus for genetic testing.
Gene Therapy | The idea that we can replace mutated or diseases genes in a person with the normal, non diseased gene, or in some way correct genetic abnormalities.

I'm a big fan of looking at different pieces of content in this kind of format, to help keep things interesting! There are many many endocrine organs in the body.

The job of the endocrine system is to help in homeostasis and regulation of the body and works closely alongside the nervous system. In fact, there are similarities and differences between these systems! The nervous system tends to have a rapid response, but a short lived action, whereas the endocrine system tends to take a little longer to get started, but has a longer lasting effect.

You've actually come across this before - the regulation of blood pressure is controlled by the brain to regulate BP immediately, and hormones (the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone pathway) over the long term.

The word **ENDOCRINE **can be broken down into _endo- _which means inside, and _crine- _which means to secrete. Endocrine organs secrete hormones (a special chemical signal in the body) into the bloodstream, where they can travel around the body and have an action and effect on the body. This is different to exocrine glands, which secrete something onto a surface (like sweat glands secreting sweat, or the liver that secretes digestive bile onto the surface of the inside of the duodenum).

These TEXTBOOK READINGS [Chapter 10, Endocrine System, Tompkins](https://www.clinicalkey.com/student/nursing/content/book/3-s2.0-B9780729543194000111) and [Chapter 25, Organisation of the Endocrine System, Patton and Thibbodeau](https://www.clinicalkey.com/student/nursing/content/book/3-s2.0-B9780702078606000377#hl0000834) could be helpful!

8\. How is glucose stored in the body, and where?

_Just like your kitchen, you have 3 places to put glucose. The pantry is for short term storage (for ready to eats, or snacks!) where the glucose is easily available, the fridge for longer term storage (where you put ingredients, things you gotta do stuff to to make a meal), for use over the day inbetween meals, and the deep freezer, where you store things for a LONG time, and only utilse once you've run out of the easy stuff (like when you freexe leftovers for when you can't be bothered cooking, or you store a ham cos you got in cheap and are saving it for Christmas). _

_The pantry of your body is your muscle, which stores glucose as glycogen (the storage form of glucose, which creates long branching chains, kind of like starch!). The glycogen in your muscles can be used BY your muscles, and is immediately available once it is broken down. Kind of like having snacks in your pocket!_

_The fridge of your body is the liver - the liver stores glucose as glycogen as well but does so for the rest of the body, so inbetween meals, your liver can release glucose into your blood for the other parts of your body to use. That nagging hungry feeling you get after a few hours is normally your liver singalling that it's running out of stored glucose!_

_The deep freeze of your body is your fat. Glucose is converted into fatty acids for long term storage, as your can store more calories as fat than as glycogen in the same amount of space. Your body likes to have fat stores for energy, as our bodies don't know that in the winter the supermarket is still open, and you liekly have blankets and maybe a heater to keep you warm! _

17\. What is the difference between steroid and non-steroid hormones?

_The bulk of our hormones are non-steroidal. They can be made from amino acids, polypeptides or proteins and cannot cross the cell membrane, so need a cell surface receptor, and create a intracellular cascade (it is kind of the equivalent of someone coming to your door and shouting instructions!). Steroid hormones are lipid soluble, so are able to diffuse through the cell membrane and enter cells. This means that they don't need a cell surface receptor and instead can travel to the nucleus where they change gene activation. This means that they can turn genes on or off, so during puberty, our hormones actually turn genes on, which is why our bodies can change so dramatically!_

Complete the genetics glossary below. They are in no particular order, and some related words are close together in the list, or further apart!

Mitosis | The process of cell division that results in 2 genetically identical (but not necessarily functionally identical) daughter cells. These daughter cells will have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs), and they will be diploid (having 2 set of chromosomes, 1 maternal and 1 paternal).

Meiosis | The process of cell division that results in 4 genetically varied daughter cells that function as gametes (egg cells and sperm cells). Only occurs in your gonads, and each daughter cell will have 23 chromosomes (1 set) and haploid (1 set chromosomes).

Variation | The fact that humans have different versions of genes, and their complement of genes (that make up their genome) can be very different to others. This variation is important for health and wellbeing. When populations have low genetic variation, they can be more susceptible to disease and genetic issues.
Gene | A sequence of DNA that codes for a protein. That protein will carry out a function in the body!
DNA | The genetic material that contains all the instructions for the body's function.
Chromatin | DNA isn't found by itself, in the nucleus, it is package up and wound around special proteins. These proteins and DNA together are called chromatin.
Chromosome | A chromosome is a length of DNA that is inherited together - certain genes are found on certain chromosomes! Humans have 46 chromosomes, 23 from mum and 23 from dad.
Autosome | A chromosome that is not a sex chromosome and so does not contribute to genetic sex. Autosomes in humans are numbered 1-22

Sex Chromosome | A chromosome that contributes to genetic sex. In humans these are the X and Y chromosome, and most people have 2, a pair of sex chromosomes, with an X from mum, and either an X or Y from dad (but there are other genetic sex combos as well!).
Haploid | A cell with only one of each chromosome. Our gametes (eggs and sperm) are haploid and have 23 chromosomes
Diploid | A cell with 2 of each chromosome. Our body cells are diploid and have 23 pairs of chromosomes, for a total of 46 chromosomes.

Aneuploidy | When a person has an abnormal number of chromsomes - usually an extra, or missing 1. There are a few different aneuploidies, but common ones are Down Syndrome (or Trisomy 21 when a person inherits an extra chromosome 21), Turners syndrome (when a person have only 1 sex chromosome and so their genetic sex is XO), or Klinefelters syndrome (when a person has 2 X chromosomes and 1 Y chromsome).

Polyploidy | Polyploid is when something has multiple SETS of chromosomes, and can be triploid (3 copies of each chromosome), tetraploid (4) and so on. This is very rare in human reproduction, but can occur in liver and placenta cells!

Disjunction and Non-Disjunction | Disjunction is when chromosomes divide during meiosis. In meiosis 2, sister chromatids that make up a chromosome are split into 2 new chromosomes, and end up in different gametes. When this doesn't happen properly, it is called non-disjunction, and gametes end up with extra chromosomes or missing chromosomes (ie 1 gametes gets 2 chromosomes, and the other gamete made in the same division gets none!)

Cell division | The process by which a cell splits into two new cells. The parent cells must be large enough and have duplicates of their DNA and organelles so the two new cells have their own machinery.
Pro, Meta, Ana, Telophases | The different stages of mitosis (and meiosis)
Gamete | In humans, this is a haploid sex cell that will be used for sexual reproduction - a male and female gamete join to create a zygote!

Dominant | A version of a gene that is always present in a phenotype (the traits/things that we see in our body). The dominant allele is like your loud friend, if they are there, you're always going to hear them!

Recessive | A version of a gene that you only see in the phemotype or trait of a person if there is none of the dominant version. The reccessive allele is like that friend you have that everyone think is shy and quiet, but as soon as everyone leaves, they turn into the nutjob you know and love :)

Codominant | When you have codominance, you have 2 dominant alleles. So that is like having two loud friends, and they just talk over each other all the time! There are traits we have where 2 version can be expressed at the same time. The best example is human blood groups. A and B alleles are both dominant, which is why you have A blood, B blood AND AB blood which has both. O blood group is the recessive!

Incomplete Dominance | Incomplete dominance is when you have two alleles, and neither one is really properly dominant. A good example is flowers, where you have a red version, and a white version of the gene for colour, but when you have BOTH versions you end up with pink! SO not quite red, not quite white. You dont see this much in humans, Sickle Cell disease is really the only example. In Sickle cell disease, if you have both a normal gene and a disease gene, half your RBCS are sickle shaped and half are normal. This mix means a person won't have the symptoms of sickle cell disease (which is bad), but! they are resistant to malaria!
Monogenic | When 1 gene creates a trait. Some examples of monogenic traits are: Attached or unattached ear lobes, middle digit hair, where there distinct options, or groups of traits.

Polygenic | When multiple genes create a trait. Some examples of polygenetic traits are things that have a spectrum, like height, body size, hair colour, body shape, eye colour, voice, skin colour \- there isn't necessarily specific groups, e.g. blonde vs brown is subjective.

Allele | Are what we call the different versions of genes, and they can be recessive or dominant! For example, a gene could have a normal and diseased version - they would each be alleles. We commonly use eye colour alleles to think about this too.
Genotype | These are the genes you got. For example, a person might have an A allele and an O allele for their blood type.
Phenotype | This is the trait you have - what you can see. The person above, with AO alleles for blood type would have Type A Blood.
Trait | The trait is something that you are inheriting from your parents, and it based on your genes
Mutation | Mutation is caused when something causes your DNA to change. Things like UV rays can cause mutations in your DNA sequence.
Zygote | When an egg and sperm join together, they form a zygote, the beginning of a new organism.
Homozygote | When you have two alleles that are the same
Heterozygote | When you have two alleles that are different
Punnet Square (Aka Monohybrid Cross) | A methods to figure out what genotypes are possible in children of two parents
Pedigree Chart | A family tree of the genes of different people. We can use these to figure out the genotypes of different people in a family based on the phenotypes of different people.
Karyotype | A diploid complement of homologous chromosomes - all the chromosomes you have in each cell! ![](https://cdn.arstechnica.net/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/nci-vol-2721-300.jpg)

Mitochondrial DNA | Your mitochondria have their own DNA! People only inherit their mitochondrial DNA from their mum, so mitochondrial DNA diseases only pass from mother to child. There is an article here [Article: Sperm Mitophagy and Mitochondrial DNALinks to an external site.](https://www.publish.csiro.au/RD/RD17364) about how any sperm mitochondria is destroyed so only egg mitochondria are found in the new zygote!

### 2\. As a nurse, you'll have many instances when knowledge about blood vessels will be relevant. Choose ONE of A to F and explain as fully as you can why you need to learn about the chosen topic.

I chose F. Blood Pressure because it is a vital skill that nurses use every day in clinical practice. Nurses regularly measure and monitor blood pressure to assess a patient's cardiovascular health and identify signs of illness or complications. Understanding blood pressure helps nurses recognize conditions such as hypertension (high blood pressure), hypotension (low blood pressure), heart disease, and shock.

Knowledge of blood vessels is important because blood pressure reflects the force of blood against the walls of the arteries. If blood vessels become narrowed, blocked, or less flexible, blood pressure can increase and place extra strain on the heart. By understanding how blood moves through the blood vessels, nurses can better interpret blood pressure readings and respond appropriately.

In addition, nurses use blood pressure measurements to evaluate the effectiveness of medications, monitor patients before and after surgery, assess emergency situations, and track changes in a patient's condition over time. Accurate blood pressure assessment can help prevent serious complications such as stroke, heart attack, and kidney damage.

For these reasons, learning about blood pressure is essential for nursing practice. It enables nurses to provide safe, effective care and make informed decisions that support patient health and well-being.

2\. Understanding blood pressure is essential to nursing practice because it's one of the vital signs I'll assess on nearly every patient, in nearly every setting. Knowing that systolic pressure reflects the force of blood during a heartbeat and diastolic reflects the pressure between beats helps me interpret a reading rather than just recording a number. Recognizing the ranges — normal, prehypertension, and the stages of hypertension — lets me identify patients at risk and know when a reading requires immediate escalation, such as a hypertensive crisis needing emergency care. This knowledge also informs medication administration (e.g., holding antihypertensives if a patient's pressure is already low), patient education (helping patients understand lifestyle changes to manage their BP), and early detection of complications like shock or hemorrhage, where blood pressure changes are often one of the first warning signs. In short, blood pressure isn't just a number to chart — it's a window into a patient's cardiovascular status that guides real-time clinical decisions.

As a nurse, understanding blood pressure is essential because measuring and interpreting blood pressure is a routine part of patient assessment. Blood pressure reflects the force of blood pushing against the walls of the arteries as the heart pumps. A normal blood pressure indicates that the heart and blood vessels are working effectively, while abnormal readings may indicate underlying health problems.Knowledge of blood pressure helps nurses identify conditions such as hypertension (high blood pressure), which increases the risk of stroke, heart attack, kidney disease, and heart failure. It also helps identify hypotension (low blood pressure), which may result from dehydration, blood loss, infection, or certain medications and can reduce blood flow to vital organs.

Nurses must also understand factors that affect blood pressure, including age, exercise, stress, medications, pain, hydration, and existing medical conditions. This knowledge enables nurses to recognise changes from a patient's normal readings and respond appropriately.Nurses need to assess blood pressure before and after giving these medicines to ensure they are safe and effective. It is also essential for monitoring patients before, during, and after surgery, during emergencies, and when caring for patients with chronic conditions such as diabetes or cardiovascular disease.

Overall, learning about blood pressure enables nurses to detect early signs of illness, monitor treatment effectiveness, make informed clinical decisions, and provide safe, evidence-based care. Accurate assessment and interpretation of blood pressure play a vital role in protecting patient health and preventing serious complications.

Nurses measure blood pressure as part of routine observations to assess how well the heart and blood vessels are supplying blood and oxygen to the body's tissues. Abnormal blood pressure can be an early sign of deterioration, so recognising changes allows nurses to respond quickly and provide appropriate care. Knowledge of blood vessels helps nurses understand why blood pressure changes. For example, narrowed arteries caused by atherosclerosis can increase blood pressure, while excessive blood loss or dehydration can cause blood pressure to drop. Nurses also use blood pressure readings to monitor the effects of medications such as antihypertensives and intravenous fluids, helping to determine whether treatment is effective.
