Blood pressure depends on the cardiac output, stroke volume, vascular resistance, blood volume, heart rate, vessel diameter, contractility, and arterial elasticity; systolic pressure is the highest pressure in the arteries when the ventricles contract and pump blood out of the heart; diastolic pressure is the lowest pressure in the arteries when the ventricles relax and fill with blood; Hypertension: sustained elevated arterial pressure of 140/90 mm Hg or higher Chronic elevation is a major cause of heart failure, vascular disease, renal failure, stroke; hypotesion: low BP, systolic pressure is below 100 mm Hg
2\. systolic: 100- 140 mmHg; diastolic: 60-90 mmHg. Normal BP: 120/80 mmHg
3\. Long-term high BP damages the arteries and makes the heart work harder; it can cause atherosclerosis, angina, heart attack, heart failure, stroke, kidney disease, and eye damage.

4\. Quinapril is an ACE inhibitor that blocks RAAS. So blocks the formation of Angiotensin 2. Angiotensin II would have increased PR by constricting the blood vessels and SV, through the release of aldosterone and ADH, causing sodium and water retention. Blocking the formation of angiotensin 2 therefore reduces fluid retention and vasoconstriction. It is effective because SV and Pr are both lowered, thereby reducing CO. Metoprolol is a beta-1 blocker. Negative inotropic, reduces the power of contraction of the heart and thereby SV; also negative chronotropic, reduces HR; CO is reduced dramatically since both SV and HR are reduced.

The cutout section of the heart wall shows the outer fibrous pericardium and the parietal and visceral layers of the serous pericardium (with the pericardial space between them). Note that a layer of fatty connective tissue is located between the visceral layer of the serous pericardium (epicardium) and the myocardium. Note also that the endocardium covers beamlike projections of myocardial muscle tissue, called _trabeculae carneae._
**STRUCTURES IN THE RIGHT HALF OF THE HEART**
**PECTINATE MUSCLES:** The ridges just to the right of the probe -their function is beautifully described by _"it acts like an accordion"_ enlarging and reducing the size of the atria.
In the photograph below the pectinate muscles in the **left atrium** are shown clearly to the top left of the photo.
**FOSSA OVALES** \- The scar forming when the fetal **foramen ovale** closes soon after birth.
1. **Fossa ovalis****-** scar tissue that formed after the foramen ovale in the fetus closed soon after birth
2. **Inferior vena cava****-** returning deoxygenated blood from lower parts of the body
3. **Coronary sinus****-** returning deoxygenated blood from the myocardium
4. **Pectinate muscles****-** named after its shape- pectinate= "like teeth of comb" parallel muscle columns in the inner wall of both atria for extra reinforcement and stretch
**4= chorda tendineae****-** Thread-like bands of fibrous tissue which attach on one end to the edges of the tricuspid and mitral valves of the heart and on the other end to the papillary muscles
5. **Papillary muscles****-** small muscles within the heart that serve to anchor the valves****

6. **Trabeculae carneae****-** Muscular ridges projecting from the inner walls of the ventricles and crisscrossing them. They prevent suction within the heart as would have happened with flat surfaces. They also help to anchor the atrioventricular valves and strengthen the heart wall.
7. **Tricuspid valve cusp (flap)****–** Together the three flaps of the tricuspid valve prevent backflow of blood from the right ventricle to the right atrium.
**STRUCTURES IN THE LEFT HALF OF THE HEART**

Check how robust the chordae tendineae and valve flaps in the left part of the heart is in comparison with those in the right half. One cuts through the flap of the bicuspid valve to see the aorta, the aortic valve with the ostea for the coronary arteries just above it.
* **Pulmonary veins (4 of them) -** returning oxygenated blood from the lungs
* **D. Pectinate muscles****-** named after its shape- pectinate= "like teeth of comb" parallel muscle columns in the inner wall of both atria for extra reinforcement and stretch
* **E = Left atrium -** receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and contracts to send it through the mitral (bicuspid valve) to the left ventricle
* ****B = Papillary muscles****-** small muscles within the heart that serve to anchor the valves**
* **C= chorda tendineae****-** Thread-like bands of fibrous tissue which attach on one end to the edges of the tricuspid and mitral valves of the heart and on the other end to the papillary muscles
* **F = Left ventricle** lined with smooth endocardium

* **G = Trabeculae carneae****-** Muscular ridges projecting from the inner walls of the ventricles and crisscrossing them. They prevent suction within the heart as would have happened with flat surfaces. They also help to anchor the atrioventricular valves and strengthen the heart wall.
* **Bicuspid valve cusp (flap), also known as the MITRAL VALVE****–** Together the two flaps of the bicuspid valve prevent backflow of blood from the left ventricle to the left atrium.
* **H = Semilunar aortic valve** \- closing to prevent backflow of blood from the aorta to the left ventricle when the heart relaxes
* **I = Aorta** \- largest artery in the body and takes oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the whole body including the heart
* **J =Brachiocephalic artery** \- branches to form **common carotid artery** to the Right side of the head, neck and brain and the **right subclavian artery** to the right shoulder and arm.

**1.1 The pectinate and trabecular muscles in the heart? What are their functions?**
**1.2 The aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves?**
**2\. What are the papillary muscles and what is their function?**
**3\. Heart sounds can be heard when the semilunar and atrioventricular valves CLOSE. It sounds like LUB-DUB. Which closure makes the LUB sound and which one the DUB sound? **
**4\. Extra sounds are called murmurs. What may cause heart murmurs? **

**1.1 The pectinate and trabecular muscles in the heart?The pectinate muscle is located in the atria, especially right atrium and trabecular muscles are in the ventricles. What are their functions? The pectinate muscles help atrial contractions and the muscular ridges in the trabeculae carneae helps ventricular contraction and prevent the ventricular walls from sticking together. **

**1.2 The aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves?The aortic semilunar valve is located between the left ventricle and the aorta. This prevents the backflow of oxygenated blood into the left ventricle. The pulmonary semilunar valve is located between pulmonary artery and the right ventricle. This prevents the backflow of deoxygenated blood into the right ventricle. **

**1.3 The visceral and parietal pericardium? The visceral pericardium is the inner serous layer directly adhering to the outer surface of the heart muscle. The patietal pericardium is the outer serous layer lining the inner surface of the fibrous pericardium.**

**1.4 Pericardium, epicardium and endocardium? Pericardium is the double-walled sac that surrounds, protects and anchors the heart. Epicardium is the outermost layer of the heart wall which is identical to visceral serous pericardium. Endocardium is the innermost layer of the heart wall, made of smooth simple squamous epithelium(endothelium) that lines heart chamber and covers the valves. **

**1.5 The tricuspid and mitral valve? The tricuspid valve is located between right atrium and right ventricle. This prevents the backflow of the deoxygenated blood into the right atrium. The mitral valve is located between the left atrium and the left ventricle. This prevents the backflow of the oxygenated blood into the left atrium. **

**1.6 The semilunar and atrioventricular valves? The atrioventricular valves are situated between the atria and the ventricles. They prevent the backflow of the blood into the atria during ventricular contractions. They are attached to the chordae tendineae and the papillary muscles. The semilunar valves are located between major arteries and the ventricles. They prevent the backflow of the blood into the ventricles during ventricular relaxation. They do not have chordae tendineae and papillary muscles. **

**2\. What are the papillary muscles and what is their function? Papillary muscles are finger-like muscular projections extending from the trabeculae careae, and they are connected to the chordae tendineae. They are tall muscles sticking out from the trabeculae carneae, which are connected to the chordae tendineae. They support the atrioventricular valves by anchoring these valves via chordae tendineae during ventricular contraction, preventing the valves from inverting into the atria and causing backflow. **

**3\. Heart sounds can be heard when the semilunar and atrioventricular valves CLOSE. It sounds like LUB-DUB. Which closure makes the LUB sound and which one the DUB sound? The LUB sound is caused by the closure of the atrioventricular valves at the start of ventricular contraction. DUB sound is caused by the closure of the semilunar valves when the ventricles begin to relax. **

**4\. Extra sounds are called murmurs. What may cause heart murmurs? Heart murmurs are caused by the turbulent blood flow within the heart. Common causes include valvular stenosis, valvular incompetence or regurgitation and congenital heart defects. **

Vicky's 15‐year‐old second cousin one removed was admitted to hospital in January 2024. He complained of a swollen chest wall for 3 months before admission and painless multiple cutaneous nodules with a history of watery discharge in the anterior chest wall, which had progressively increased in size. This was associated with an on‐and‐off fever, night sweats, and anorexia with more than a 6‐kg loss of weight over the previous 3 months. The patient also had bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, showing no signs of improvement after a broad‐spectrum antibiotics treatment prescribed by the general practitioner. The circulatory system consists of the cardiovascular system and the lymphatic system. The cardiovascular system is a closed, high-pressure circulatory system with the heart acting as a central pump, whereas the lymphatic system is an open, low-pressure circulatory system with no central pump ([1](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.04.090#bib1)). The lymphatic vessels are present in almost all tissues except bone marrow, cartilage, and cornea ([1](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.04.090#bib1)). Several liters of fluids are filtered via the semipermeable membrane of the capillaries into the interstitial space every day. The filtered fluid has important physiological functions, such as tissue nutrition and hydration. An increase in the amount of the filtered fluid can lead to interstitial edema with clinical manifestations such as extremity and tissue edema, including pulmonary edema.

The lymphatic system is an integral part of the circulatory system and plays an important role in the**volume homeostasis** of the human body. The complex anatomy and physiology paired with a lack of simple diagnostic tools to study the lymphatic system have led to an underappreciation of the contribution of the lymphatic system to acute and chronic heart failure (HF). Herein, we discuss the physiological role of the lymphatic system in volume management and the evidence demonstrating the dysregulation of the lymphatic system in HF. Further, we discuss the opportunity to target the lymphatic system in the management of HF and different potential approaches to accessing the lymphatic system. ![gr1 \(1\)-1.jpg](https://canvas.manukau.ac.nz/courses/61986/files/8819416/preview?verifier=xx0r4tWY08hZr1XRpw2Dlm2ywKzILJS0hbnt4sHL)

Lymph contains high concentrations of proteins that are involved in cell catabolism and apoptosis, extracellular matrix remodeling, and innate immunity ([3](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.04.090#bib3)). Besides its role in **fluid homeostasis** , lymph acts as a chemical buffer system, facilitates immune cell trafficking, and transports proteomes to draining lymph nodes ([3](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.04.090#bib3)).

Lymph is returned to the cardiovascular system through 2 major lymphatic ducts that empty into the venous system (ie, the right lymphatic duct, and the thoracic duct) ([4](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.04.090#bib4)). The right lymphatic duct drains lymph from the right side of the thorax, right upper extremity, and right side of the head and neck, and empties into the junction of the right internal jugular vein and the right subclavian vein ([Figure 2](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.04.090#fig2)) ([4](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.04.090#bib4)). The thoracic duct runs superiorly from the superior aspect of the cisterna chyli to the lower cervical spine, drains lymph from all the body except parts that are drained by the right lymphatic duct, and empties into the junction of the left internal jugular vein and the left subclavian vein ([5](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.04.090#bib5)). The thoracic duct terminates as a single duct in the majority of cases (72%), or less frequently as double (8.5%), triple (1.8%), or quadruple (2.2%) ducts ([6](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.04.090#bib6)). The thoracic duct typically returns approximately 1.38 mL/kg/h of lymph to the central venous circulation ([5](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.04.090#bib5)). An increase in the filtration volume (arterial/venous congestion) is counteracted with an increase in the amount of filtered lymph fluid and a decrease in interstitial protein, thus decreasing the oncotic pressure of the interstitium ([7](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.04.090#bib7)).

## Mechanisms of Lymphatic Congestion in HF

Similar to venous congestion, lymphatic congestion is a hallmark of Heart failure (HF) and drives both symptom manifestation and adverse outcomes in this population. In HF, a number of parallel mechanisms contribute to the **accumulation of interstitial fluid** , which manifests itself clinically as **lower and upper extremity edema, pulmonary edema, hepatic congestion** with subsequent **ascites, renal failure, and increased gut permeability and decreased absorption** ([16](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.04.090#bib16)) ([Central Illustration](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2021.04.090#undfig2)).
Mechanisms of lymphatic dysfunction in heart failure- shortened
1. | Increased filtration due to**higher capillary hydrostatic pressure** due to venous congestion in the tissue

2. | **Decreased drainage** due to an **increase in central venous pressure (CVP)** that prevents the emptying of lymph via the thoracic duct into the central venous circulation. This process depends on a negative pressure gradient from tissue → thoracic duct → central veins.

3. | **Increased vascular permeability**(aka, vascular leakage) enhances the extravasation of plasma and protein with resultant accumulation of interstitial fluid since heart failure is characterized by a systemic pro-inflammatory state which increases vascular permeability caused by disintegration of the vascular barrier; thus, large molecules, such as proteins, can leak into the interstitial space**** decreasing the oncotic pressure of plasma and increases the interstitial oncotic pressure**,** with a net increase in filtration volume.
4. | Lymphatic vessels contain lymphatic valves, which regulate a unidirectional lymph flow. **Dysfunction of the lymphatic valves** can lead to lymph reflux and lymphedema.
5. | **Elevated inferior vena cava pressure** in heart failure (HF) leads to elevated **renal vein pressure** leading to increased sodium and fluid retention in HF.
6. | ** Insufficient formation of new lymph vessels** (eg, after myocardial infarction) can lead to myocardial interstitial fibrosis, cardiac remodeling, and cardiac dysfunction.

Academic integrity encompasses values of honesty, fairness, trustworthiness, and respect and is essential in all student conduct and assessments. It is important that students demonstrate academic integrity in all assessments to ensure that their own original work is submitted. Plagiarism occurs when the values of academic integrity are disregarded and students submit other people's ideas, theories, opinions, illustrations, and graphics as their own. The School of Nursing has a strong commitment to fostering academic integrity to support student success across all programmes.
Academic integrity involves values such as responsibility, honesty, fairness, respect, and trust towards your own academic study and assessment.

12.2.1 Students must behave honestly in all summative assessment. All work presented by students for summative assessment must reflect their own learning, have been substantively written or authored by them, and be their own work (unless formally referenced and acknowledged - see section 12.3: Plagiarism and plagiarism detection software). Work must not be submitted elsewhere in any other programme, training scheme or course unless otherwise permitted by the Head of School.
12.2.2 Notwithstanding section 12.2.1, work may be presented by a group of students for summative assessment where this is specified in the assessment information.

12.2.3 MIT treats misconduct during assessment very seriously. Misconduct during assessment is defined in the Glossary (see section 23: Glossary) and involves any attempt by a student to gain an unfair advantage in a summative assessment (including cheating and plagiarism) or sharing of information about a summative assessment. Suspected incidents of misconduct during assessment will be dealt with in accordance with section 13: Misconduct and, if an investigation is required, the investigation will be carried out in accordance with section 15: Misconduct and Complaints Investigations.
Plagiarism is the representation of another author's language, thoughts, ideas, or expressions as one's own original work.
12.3.1 Plagiarism is regarded as misconduct during assessment (see section 13: Misconduct) and is forbidden.

12.3.2 Plagiarism is using someone else’s work without indicating that the ideas are not your own. Plagiarism may be either intentional or unintentional. It involves paraphrasing or copying information (e.g. from books, journal articles, electronic sources such as the internet or databases, sound recordings, films, other students, your own previous work) without appropriately acknowledging/referencing the source.
12.3.3 All cited material must be formally referenced and acknowledged. Guidelines for appropriately referencing and acknowledging other people’s work are available from each School and the Library.

12.3.4 To check academic integrity, MIT may use plagiarism-detection software (e.g. Turnitin) or other means to confirm that a summative assessment is a student’s own work and/or compare two or more of a student’s summative assessment submissions (to ensure an assessment has not been submitted previously for assessment – see section 12.2.1: Academic integrity). Work may be retained on a plagiarism-detection database for on-going comparison with other work submitted.

12.3.5 By enrolling in a course at MIT, students agree to their work being submitted to plagiarism-detection software for checking. Declining to allow the use of the plagiarism-detection software by MIT could result in a student being unable to complete a programme, training scheme or course.

Within the nursing programme, the content is designed to be delivered using a blended delivery option, which includes both onsite (campus) and online delivery. Professional behaviour is expected when engaging in both forms of delivery. To make the most of your learning during your online classes, there are some guidelines to support you to have the best learning experience online.

Online meetings are now part of our lives in education. The challenges and benefits of video conferencing can be much different than in-person meetings, meaning that the rules, or code of conduct that we need to follow during online meetings are often different as well.
Explore what Netiquette is and how to apply it while you're online.

* Be on time: With the benefit of taking your meetings from anywhere, it is especially important that you are on time for your online meetings. Plan ahead, and make sure that you are ready, able to log in, be ready with your computer a few minutes before the meeting starts.
* Professional dress code: be fully dressed, it is not professional to present in inappropriate dress wear (eg Pyjamas).

* Use Video: Keeping your video on during an Online meeting. Seeing all nursing students (and your colleagues/ lecturer) on a video call will help cue people into others' reactions, and will make the meeting more engaging for everyone involved. Where this is not possible (due to poor connection) please inform the lecturer beforehand via email.
* Communication: It is essential that you converse online in a polite and professional manner. Use the virtual ‘raised hand’ if you wish to be included in the online / video discussion during class.
* If possible choose a professional or blurred background when using online forums.
* Use the chat box if you need to make a statement, however, remember it is public to the class.
* When you’re not talking, make sure to mute yourself. Background noise is very distracting to other nursing students.

* Avoid multitasking: Be professionals & resist the temptation to multi-task. It is not professional for a student nurse to be multi-tasking e.g. checking your email or working on another project, drinking, eating, smoking or vaping is not acceptable. Treat an online meeting like a face-to-face meeting, and give it your undivided attention.

**SYNOVIAL JOINT** | **ANTAGONISTIC MUSCLE PAIRS** | **HAVERSIAN SYSTEM IN COMPACT BONE**
**Comparison of endochondral and Intramembranous ossification processes**
#### 1.**Development of the Ossification Center:** Mesenchymal cells differentiate to become osteoblasts that start to make osteoid forming a primary ossification centre.

#### 2\. **Calcification of Osteoid:** Osteoblasts secrete **osteoid** (unmineralized matrix), which hardens within a few days as calcium is deposited. As the matrix calcifies, entrapped osteoblasts differentiate into **osteocytes**.

#### **3\. Formation of Trabecular (Spongy) Bone:** As osteoid forms, it surrounds embryonic blood vessels, forming a lattice of trabecular bone. The vascularized connective tissue surrounding the bone differentiates into red bone marrow.

#### **4\. Development of the Periosteum and Compact Bone:** Mesenchymal cells at the surface condense to form the **periosteum**. The periosteum produces a thin layer of compact bone (cortical bone) over the surface of the spongy bone.

1. #### **Development of Cartilage Model:** Mesenchymal cells differentiate into chondroblasts, which produce a hyaline cartilage template, shaped like the future bone, surrounded by a membrane called the perichondrium.
2. #### **Growth of the Cartilage Model:** Chondroblasts become trapped in the matrix and are called chondrocytes. The cartilage model grows in length and thickness.

3. #### **Bony Collar Formation:** Blood vessels invade the perichondrium, triggering cells to differentiate into osteoblasts. These osteoblasts create a collar of compact bone around the diaphysis (shaft).
4. #### **Primary Ossification Center Development:** Chondrocytes in the center hypertrophy (enlarge) and calcify the surrounding matrix. As they die due to lack of nutrients, they leave cavities.

5. #### **Vascular Invasion & Medullary Cavity Formation:** Blood vessels, osteoblasts, and osteoclasts (the "periosteal bud") invade the center, forming the primary ossification center. Osteoblasts replace calcified cartilage with spongy bone. Osteoclasts break down this bone to form the medullary cavity.

6. #### **Secondary Ossification Centers:** Similar to the primary center, vascular invasion occurs at the epiphyses (ends of the bone) shortly before or after birth, creating secondary ossification centers.

7. #### **Epiphyseal Plate & Articular Cartilage Formation:** Hyaline cartilage remains in two places: covering the joint surface (articular cartilage) and between the epiphysis and diaphysis (epiphyseal or growth plate), allowing for further longitudinal growth.

* 2.1 Conduction zone: Nasal cavity, Pharynx, Trachea, Bronchi, Larger bronchioles, provides passageway for air to reach the alveoli, Cleans, warms, and moistens inspired air.
* 2.2 Respiratory zone: Terminal bronchioles or alveoli, Site of actual gas exchange.
* 3.1 alveoli: Approximately 300 million alveoli: most of lungs’ volume provide tremendous surface area for gas exchange
* 3.2 respiratory mucosa is the moist lining that covers most of the respiratory tract, especially the nasal cavity, trachea, and bronchi.
* 3.3 mucus is a thick, sticky fluid produced by goblet cells and mucus glands in the respiratory tract.

* 3.4 red blood cell (erythrocyte): It carries oxygen from the lungs to body tissues. It carries some **carbon dioxide** from body tissues back to the lungs. It helps maintain the acid–base balance of the blood.****

EXAMPLES | Pelvis, cranium, scapula, ribs, sternum | Femur (longest), Tibia, humerus, radius, ulna, fibula Phalanges, Metacarpals
DESCRIPTION | Two layers of compact bone with trabecular/ spongy bone between them. Surrounded by periosteal membrane |
* Longitudinal cylindrical shape with diaphysis (shafts)in middle part and epiphyses (heads) at the ends.
* Compact bone on outside of whole bone and and spongy bone towards epiphyses.
* Medullary cavity in centre of diaphysis with yellow marrow in it.
* Spongy bone houses red marrow - blood cells are formed here.
* Bone (except where it articulates with other bones) is covered with periosteum (linking bone to blood supply- Sharpeys fibres between periosteum and bone)
* Epiphyses at ends are covered with hyaline cartilage that reduces friction in joints.
* The medullary cavity is lined by an endosteum.
· POSITION OF SPONGY BONE | BETWEEN LAYERS OF COMPACT BONE | TOWARDS THE EPIPHYSES
HAPPENS IN CARTILAGE/ MEMBRANE | · Membrane · INTRAMEBRANOUS OSSIFICATION | · hyaline cartilage · ENDOCHONDRAL OSSIFICATION

STEPS IN OSSIFICATION PROCESS | · Starts as a membrane · Ossification centres form in membrane · Bloodvessels connect from periosteum to ossification centres Osteoblasts form compact bone on outside | · Starts as cartilage model · Formation of bony collar · Cavitation (formation of cavity) · Bloodvessels -provide nutrients · Primary centre – ossify -diaphysis · Secondary centres -epiphyses Hyaline cartilage is replaced by bone -only remains at tips and at epiphyseal plate

* **Electrical Conduction system of the heart:** a network of specialised nodes (groups of cells) ensuring that myocardial contractions happen in a coordinated, rhythmic pattern:
* The left and right bundle branches.

* **Cardiac muscle:** Unique features: Automaticity/ electrogenic, Conductivity, Intercalated discs ( gap junctions), Syncytium (many cells acting as multinucleated unit), muscle bridges connecting fibres into integrated unit
* **Cardiac output (CO)** = Stroke volume (SV) x Heart rate (HR)
* **Blood pressure (BP)** = SV x HR x Peripheral resistance (PR)
* Mechanisms used by the body to keep blood pressure in a safe range:
* **Neural mechanism** = Baro receptor reflex. Baroreceptors found in carotid sinus and aortic arch, stretch receptors that monitors blood pressure-

* **Blood pressure high-** ->sends frequent impulses to cardiac centre in Medulla oblongata --> causes inhibition of cardiac acceleratory centre and stimulation of cardiac inhibitory centre--> parasympathetic nervous system activated slowing heart down (acetylcholine released).

* **Blood pressure low** \-->sends frequent impulses to cardiac centre in Medulla oblongata --> causes stimulation of cardiac acceleratory centre and inhibition of cardiac inhibitory centre-->sympathetic nervous system activated speeding heart up (catecholamines released).

* for further info see: [MODULE 1.1: Homeostatic Mechanisms: Regulation of Blood Pressure - THE BULLET POINTS](https://canvas.manukau.ac.nz/courses/61986/pages/module-1-dot-1-homeostatic-mechanisms-regulation-of-blood-pressure-the-bullet-points "MODULE 1.1: Homeostatic Mechanisms: Regulation of Blood Pressure - THE BULLET POINTS")

Explain the respiratory response in acidosis and alkalosis (2)
* In acidosis (**low pH - below 7.35, high CO₂)**(1/2) breathing **becomes faster and deeper ( 1/2) **to remove CO₂.
* In**** alkalosis**(high pH, above 7.45, low CO** ₂) (1/2) **breathing slows and becomes shallower**(1/2) to retain CO₂, helping balance blood pH.

Question: Acidosis and Alkalosis bring about changes in breathing. Analyse the changes in breathing patterns brought about by respiratory issues and metabolic issues respectively by using a table. Make sure that you indicate whether the breathing pattern is caused by the change in pH or used as a compensatory method to deal with it.(6).
Condition | Primary Breathing Change | Cause/Compensation | P CO2 Level Normal 35-45 mm Hg
**Respiratory Acidosis** | Hypoventilation is causing Respiratory acidosis (Slow/Shallow)(1/2) | **Cause:** Lungs cannot remove CO2 (1/2) | Increased (>45 mmHg)(1/2)
**Metabolic Acidosis** | Kussmaul Breathing (hyperventilation is compensating for metabolic acidosis) (Deep/Rapid)(1/2) | **Compensation:** To blow off CO2 (1/2) | Decreased (<35 mmHg)(1/2)
**Respiratory Alkalosis** | Hyperventilation (Fast/Deep)(1/2) | **Cause:** Excess CO2 removal(1/2) | Decreased (<35 mmHg)(1/2)
**Metabolic Alkalosis** | Hypoventilation (Slow)(1/2) | **Compensation:** To retain CO2 (1/2) | Increased (>45 mmHg)(1/2)
QUESTION: Use the framework for reflex actions to analyse the response of the respiratory system to increased pH of the blood. (4).

If the blood pH increases, receptors(1/2) (peripheral and central chemoreceptors)(1/2) will pick it up. They will sent impulses via a sensory neuron (1/2) to the integrative centres (1/2) (respiratory centres in the medulla and pons)(1/2) . From there impulses will be sent via motor neurons (1/2) to the effectors (1/2) (the breathing muscles).(1/2)

QUESTION: Use the framework for reflex actions to analyse the response of the respiratory system to increased pH of the blood. (4).

If the blood pH increases, receptors(1/2) (peripheral and central chemoreceptors)(1/2) will pick it up. They will sent impulses via a sensory neuron (1/2) to the integrative centres (1/2) (respiratory centres in the medulla and pons)(1/2) . From there impulses will be sent via motor neurons (1/2) to the effectors (1/2) (the breathing muscles).(1/2)

#### **THE LAST OF THE DAILY RECAPS -WEEK 1 ONLY**
* **Electrical Conduction system of the heart:** a network of specialised nodes (groups of cells) ensuring that myocardial contractions happen in a coordinated, rhythmic pattern:
* The left and right bundle branches.

* **Cardiac muscle:** Unique features: Automaticity/ electrogenic, Conductivity, Intercalated discs ( gap junctions), Syncytium (many cells acting as multinucleated unit), muscle bridges connecting fibres into integrated unit
* **Cardiac output (CO)** = Stroke volume (SV) x Heart rate (HR)
* **Blood pressure (BP)** = SV x HR x Peripheral resistance (PR)
* Mechanisms used by the body to keep blood pressure in a safe range:
* **Neural mechanism** = Baro receptor reflex. Baroreceptors found in carotid sinus and aortic arch, stretch receptors that monitors blood pressure-

* **Blood pressure high-** ->sends frequent impulses to cardiac centre in Medulla oblongata --> causes inhibition of cardiac acceleratory centre and stimulation of cardiac inhibitory centre--> parasympathetic nervous system activated slowing heart down (acetylcholine released).

* **Blood pressure low** \-->sends frequent impulses to cardiac centre in Medulla oblongata --> causes stimulation of cardiac acceleratory centre and inhibition of cardiac inhibitory centre-->sympathetic nervous system activated speeding heart up (catecholamines released).

* for further info see: [MODULE 1.1: Homeostatic Mechanisms: Regulation of Blood Pressure - THE BULLET POINTS](https://canvas.manukau.ac.nz/courses/61986/pages/module-1-dot-1-homeostatic-mechanisms-regulation-of-blood-pressure-the-bullet-points "MODULE 1.1: Homeostatic Mechanisms: Regulation of Blood Pressure - THE BULLET POINTS")

**2\. Large blood vessels of the body.**
* * Check CVS 1 Powerpoint to help you to label page 19 onwards in your lab book;
* Blood vessels are usually symmetrical- left and right renal arteries and left and right renal veins;
* Blood vessels often carry the name of bones or organs- pulmonary for lungs, femoral for close to femur, subclavian for "beneath the clavicle", etc.

* Pay special attention to blood vessels that are unique- e.g. **carotid** **arteries** take blood to the head and brain, **jugular veins** return blood from head and brain; both **R and L brachiocephalic veins,** but only **R brachiocephalic artery** which then branches into a right carotid and subclavian artery. Today we learned about the heart:
* * * 4 chambers (2 atria= receiving blood, 2 ventricles =pumping blood)
* 4 valves: the AV's make "lub" when they close and blood bumps into them and the semi lunar ones make "dub".
* 2 ostia for coronary arteries that branch off aorta right distal to the aortic valve.
* 3 veins bringing deoxygenated blood to right atrium: IVC, SVC and Coronary sinus (from heart muscle)
* 4 veins bringing oxygenated blood to left atrium. 2 left pulmonary veins from left lung, 2 right pulmonary veins from right lung.
* 1 artery, pulmonary trunk (splitting in 2 pulmonary arteries) leave right ventricle.
* Left ventricle has very thick myocardium (cardiac muscle layer). It must pump blood to whole body.
* Right ventricle has thinner myocardium. It pumps blood only to lungs.
* The heart is situated in the
* inferior of the large blood vessels,
* It's apex is located slightly to the left of the midline in the cardiac notch on the left lung.
* The heart and visceral pericardium are surrounded by the pericardial space
* The myocardium is provided with oxygen and nutrients by the
* right and left coronary arteries, first branches of aorta.
* They branch to give rise to several arteries of which BN2 must take note of the
* All coronary veins drain into the coronary sinus which takes deoxygenated blood to the right atrium.
* CO =Cardiac output = blood delivered by heart per minute
* SV =blood delivered by heart per second
* PR =resistance of arterial walls to blood coming into them

* have prominent internal elastic laminas (zig-zag layer) in tunica intima to be able to respond to the changing pressure because of the the heart pumping blood into them (systole) and then relaxing (diastole);

* thick tunica media with smooth muscles;and

DISCUSSION PROMPT: MODULE 1.1: TEST CASE STUDY 1: BLOOD PRESSURE

Jack and Jill have blood pressure issues. Jack has high blood pressure and has been taking quinapril for about 1 year, and their GP has just added metoprolol to their prescription. Jack has been told they may need to be mindful of standing too quickly, as Jack might get a bit dizzy or even pass out; something called postural hypotension. Jack is really mindful, as their Dad had to get an angiogram and then a bypass in a coronary vessel due to blocked coronary vessels and angina. Jill, on the other hand, has been having dizzy spells, and excessive thirst. They were admitted to the hospital, and vitals were taken showing a bp of 80/55, with concentrated, low-volume urine being noted by the admitting nurse. As a student nurse, you’ll need a robust understanding of how the cardiovascular system works, to understand what is happening for each of these people.
What determines blood pressure? You’ll need to think about our physiology as well as those factors that can change our blood pressure.
High blood pressure is defined as?
High blood pressure has several chronic, downstream consequences. What are they? Thinking about the implications for long-term health and wellness, as well as why we care as nurses!
Low blood pressure has several acute consequences. These are?

You have nervous system processes that help to keep your blood pressure steady at rest and help to increase or decrease it back to normal for exercise or after exercise, based on feedback from your body. We are going to focus on
– how your body RETURNS blood pressure to normal after it has been changed

How does the nervous system detect and return blood pressure to normal when it is lower than normal (e.g. you’ve just stood up quickly and BP to your brain drops; thnx gravity – as for Jack’s postural hypotension)
How is this process different when it is higher than normal (e.g. after a run, after a fright, etc)
You also have renal system processes that use hormones to help return low blood pressure to normal over the long term.
The kidneys normally help to increase blood pressure if it is too low – this is a slower process (which takes minutes to hours, depending on the circumstances). Explain how this occurs.

The human body has what is called set points – this is where the body maintains homeostasis to, what your body thinks is normal. These set points will be slightly different between people. Sometimes, if your body has something that is constantly outside the normal range (e.g. if your BP is always high), your body changes its set point (it kind of goes, ahh fine, this is what normal is now) to your new normal. This is similar to when people from Dunedin laugh when Aucklanders say it’s cold, and they’re like, THIS ISN'T COLD UNTIL YOUR TOILET IS FROZEN, GET IN THE BIN YOU WUSS. These two individuals have different ‘set points’ about what is cold.

PRESSURE IN DIFFERENT KINDS OF VESSELS

Fluid always travels from an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure. Fluid flows from an area of high pressure in the tank (100 mmHg) toward the area of low pressure above the bucket (0 mmHg). Blood likewise tends to move from an area of high pressure at the beginning of the aorta (100 mmHg) toward the area of lowest pressure at the end of the venae cavae (0 mmHg). Blood flow between any two points in the circulatory system can always be predicted by the pressure gradient.

Blood pressure is determined by several factors related to both the heart and blood vessels. It is the force that blood exerts on the walls of arteries as it is pumped by the heart. Blood pressure is influenced by:
: The amount of blood the heart pumps per minute. The higher the cardiac output, the higher the blood pressure.
: The resistance that blood encounters as it flows through blood vessels, mainly in the arteries. If arteries constrict (narrow), resistance increases, and so does blood pressure.
: The total amount of blood in the circulatory system. More blood increases pressure.
: Thicker blood (higher viscosity) increases resistance and, consequently, blood pressure.
: Healthy, flexible arteries allow for more efficient blood flow. If the arteries become stiff (e.g., due to arteriosclerosis), blood pressure can rise.

2. What is the structure of a lymph nodes, and what is found in lymph nodes?
The lymph node is enclosed by a fibrous outer layer called the capsule. This provides structural support and protection for the node.

The outer region of the lymph node is called the cortex. The cortex contains clusters of immune cells called B lymphocytes and follicles (also called lymphoid follicles), where B-cells are activated in response to antigens.

Beneath the cortex is the paracortex, which contains T lymphocytes (T-cells). This area is also where the immune cells are activated by antigens and where interactions between B-cells and T-cells occur.

The medulla is the inner portion of the lymph node. It contains medullary cords, which are made up of lymphocytes (mainly B-cells), macrophages, and plasma cells. This is where the final steps of immune responses take place, including the production of antibodies.

The lymph node contains sinuses, which are channels that allow lymph to flow through the node. These sinuses help filter out pathogens, debris, and other foreign particles as the lymph flows through the node.

Lymph enters the node through afferent lymphatic vessels and exits through efferent lymphatic vessels. The afferent vessels bring lymph from the tissues, while the efferent vessels drain filtered lymph away from the node.
What is Found in Lymph Nodes?
B lymphocytes (B-cells): These are found primarily in the cortex and are responsible for producing antibodies in response to pathogens.
T lymphocytes (T-cells): Found mainly in the paracortex, T-cells help in recognizing and killing infected cells or coordinating the immune response.
Macrophages: Found throughout the lymph node, these cells help engulf and digest pathogens and debris.
Plasma cells: These are activated B-cells that have differentiated to secrete antibodies.

The fluid that circulates through the lymphatic system, carrying white blood cells, proteins, waste products, and sometimes pathogens or foreign particles, which the immune cells within the lymph node work to filter and destroy.

29 MIT| Nursing & Health Studies| 722.537 | 722.541 | 722.552 | 2026 (2) Section C: Electrocardiogram Much of the heart is cardiac muscle (myocardium). Unlike the skeletal muscle cells, cardiac muscle cells generate their own electrical impulses and conduct these impulses (action potentials) to the entire myocardium. These do not occur over the entire heart simultaneously; instead, different parts of the heart are depolarised to different extents at any instant in time. This causes small electric currents to flow in the extracellular fluid from one part of the body to another. These currents can be detected by placing sensitive electrodes on certain parts of the body. A recording of these currents forms an electrocardiogram (ECG). By convention, the pairs of electrodes are placed in a certain order to give a series of ECG readings. Three of these are shown below. Lead I ................................................... Left Arm-Right Arm Lead II .................................................. Right Arm-Left Leg Lead III ................................................. Left Arm-Left Leg Any potential difference (voltage) between each pair of electrodes will be amplified and then recorded by an electrocardiograph machine, as a series of up-and-down waves called deflection waves. Clinical applications • Joint surfaces, fitting perfectly into one another, are covered in hyaline cartilage to absorb shock and make movement smooth and painless. Damaged cartilage exposes bone ends so that they grind on one another, leading to the formation of bone spurs, as body tries to heal it (causing ill-fitting joint surfaces and more friction). • The periosteum plays an important role in bone growth and bone healing. 2 1. Blood pressure Jack and Jill have blood pressure issues. Jack has high blood pressure, and has been talking quinapril for about 1 year, and their GP has just added metoprolol to their prescription. Jack has been told they may need to be mindful of standing too quickly, as Jack might get a bit dizzy or even pass out; something called postural hypotension. Jack is really mindful, as their Dad had to get an angiogram, and then a bypass in a coronary vessel due to blocked coronary vessels and angina. Jill, on the other hand, has been having dizzy spells, and excessive thirst. They were admitted to hospital, and vitals were taken showing a bp of 80/55, with concentrated, low volume urine being noted by the admitting nurse. As a student nurse, you’ll need a robust understanding of how the cardiovascular system works, to understand what is happening for each of these people. 1. What determines blood pressure? You’ll need to think about our physiology as well as those factors that can change our blood pressure. 2. High blood pressure is defined as? 3. High blood pressure has several chronic, downstream consequences. What are they? Thinking about the implications for long term health and wellness, as well as why we care as nurses! 4. Low blood pressure has several acute consequences. These are? You have nervous system processes that help to keep your blood pressure steady at rest, and help to increase or decrease it back to normal for exercise or after exercise, based on feedback from your body. We are going to focus on regulation – how your body RETURNS blood pressure to normal after it has been changed. 5. How does the nervous system detect and return blood pressure to normal when it is lower than normal (e.g. you’ve just stood up quickly and BP to your brain drops; think gravity – as for Jack’s postural hypotension) 6. How is this process different when it is higher than normal (e.g. after a run, after a fright, etc) You also have renal system processes that use hormones to help return low blood pressure to normal over the long term. 7. The kidneys normally help to increase blood pressure if it is too low – this is a slower process (which takes minutes to hours, depending on the circumstances). Explain how this occurs. The human body has what is called set points – this is where the body maintains homeostasis to, what your body thinks is normal. These set points will be slightly different between people. Sometimes, if your body has something that is constantly outside the normal range (e.g. if your BP is always high), your body changes its set point (it kind of goes, ahh fine, this is what normal is now) to your new normal. This is similar to when people from Dunedin laugh when Aucklanders say it’s cold, and they’re like, THIS ISNT COLD UNTIL YOUR TOILET IS FROZEN, GET IN THE BIN YOU WUSS. These two individuals have different ‘set points’ about what is cold. 8. What are Jack’s medications trying to do? Explain in plain, easy to understand language! Atherosclerosis is the process by which blood vessels can become narrowed, because a fatty plaque builds up in the blood vessel. This narrowing can prevent blood flowing though the vessel, and even end up blocking the vessel. If this happens in the coronary vessels, this can cause angina, chest pain, or worse! 10.
